tactics.name: Model
tactics.description: The "Model" tactic, in the context of AI security, focuses on developing a comprehensive understanding and detailed mapping of all AI/ML assets, their configurations, data flows, operational behaviors, and interdependencies. This foundational knowledge is crucial for informing and enabling all subsequent defensive actions. It involves knowing precisely what AI systems exist within the organization, how they are architected, what data they ingest and produce, their critical dependencies (both internal and external), and their expected operational parameters and potential emergent behaviors.

techniques.name: AI Asset Inventory & Mapping
techniques.description: Maintain an authoritative, versioned map of the AI estate: owned models, datasets, infrastructure, dependencies, agent skills, externally consumed AI services, and public or private AI endpoints. Reconcile declared inventory with independently observed deployment, network, identity, registry, and control-plane evidence so unknown, orphaned, stale, or unexpectedly exposed assets remain visible.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns authoritative discovery, inventory, dependency mapping, ownership, and declared-versus-observed reconciliation for the AI estate. It produces stable asset facts and drift findings but does not authorize, block, remediate, contain, or evict an asset.

subTechniques.name: AI Component & Infrastructure Inventory
subTechniques.description: Systematically catalogs all AI/ML assets, including models (categorized by type, version, and ownership), datasets, software components, and the specialized hardware they run on (e.g., GPUs, TPUs). This technique focuses on creating a dynamic, up-to-date inventory to provide comprehensive visibility into all components that constitute the AI ecosystem, which is a prerequisite for accurate risk assessment and the application of targeted security controls.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns the authoritative identity, version, owner, lifecycle state, and security-relevant attributes of AI components, models, datasets, infrastructure, and accelerators.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-001.001 inventories the assets that exist; AID-M-001.002 maps the dependency edges and release composition that connect those assets.
An asset record can be complete without proving its upstream and downstream relationships, while a dependency edge must resolve to inventoried endpoints.

implementationGuidance: Establish and maintain a dynamic, up-to-date registry of AI models and datasets with security-relevant metadata.
Include specialized AI accelerators (GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, FPGAs) and their firmware versions in the AI asset inventory.
Assign clear ownership and accountability for each inventoried AI asset.
Integrate AI asset inventory with broader IT asset management and configuration management databases (CMDBs).

subTechniques.name: AI System Dependency Mapping
subTechniques.description: Systematically identifies and documents all components and services that an AI system depends on to function correctly. This includes direct software libraries, transitive dependencies, external data sources, third-party APIs, and other internal AI models or microservices. This dependency map is crucial for understanding the complete supply chain attack surface and for performing comprehensive security assessments.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns direct and transitive dependency relationships, external service and data dependencies, trust-boundary interfaces, SBOM composition, and deployed release-composition reconciliation.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-001.002 maps how components and services depend on one another; AID-M-001.001 records the authoritative identity and attributes of each asset.
Dependency completeness and asset-inventory completeness are separate claims and require different populations and evidence.

implementationGuidance: Pin every direct and transitive software dependency to an immutable reviewed version and verify that the resolved build population exactly matches the lock state.
Document every internal service, external service, model-provider API, data feed, and runtime dependency with an accountable owner and a deployable interface and trust-boundary record.
Generate a validated dependency SBOM for every releasable software artifact and bind it to the exact build inputs and output digest.
Maintain a version-controlled system and service dependency map, assemble the complete release composition, and independently read back every deployed replica.

subTechniques.name: Agentic Skill & Instruction Asset Inventory
subTechniques.description: Maintain an authoritative, versioned inventory of every installed or enabled agent skill and instruction asset across supported agent platforms. Record its canonical identifier, version and digest, source and provenance, owner, host or platform, installation path, declared permissions and capabilities, dependencies, lifecycle state, and last observed deployment. Discover the complete deployed population from agent control planes, extension registries, and relevant filesystems; reconcile it against declared records; identify unknown, duplicate, orphaned, stale, or drifted entries; preserve signed reconciliation evidence; and emit bounded findings or lifecycle triggers to the controls that own admission, retirement, containment, or eviction. OpenClaw and Claude Code skills use SKILL.md; Cursor agent skills also use SKILL.md and project rules under .cursor/rules/*.mdc. Apply the same inventory contract to equivalent platform-specific skill, rule, plugin, and workflow artifacts.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns discovery, identity, version, provenance, owner, installation state, permissions, dependencies, and declared-versus-observed reconciliation for agent skills, instruction assets, rules, plugins, and workflow artifacts. It emits lifecycle findings but does not admit, install, enforce, retire, contain, or evict them.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-001.003 inventories which skill or instruction artifact is deployed and supplies its stable identity and version; AID-D-005.004 records what an agent and those artifacts did during a session.
Inventory reconciliation does not replace event capture, and session logs do not prove the complete installed-skill population.

implementationGuidance: Establish a central skill inventory with mandatory registration for all installed skills.
Import an authoritative approval or exception decision into the inventory and bind it to the exact skill digest without making the inventory the approval or admission authority.
Run periodic reconciliation to identify orphaned, dormant, and scan-gap skills.
Ingest trusted ownership, vulnerability, publisher, and incident events; update inventory state; and emit signed, control-routed lifecycle triggers without claiming the downstream action completed.

subTechniques.name: AI Service & Embedded SaaS AI Discovery
subTechniques.description: Continuously discover externally hosted AI services, embedded SaaS AI features, browser-accessed generative AI apps, model-provider APIs, and SaaS-hosted MCP or agent endpoints used by enterprise identities, workloads, or managed devices. The objective is technical visibility: identify AI processing paths that do not appear in the declared AI asset inventory, classify whether sensitive data may be flowing into them, and produce evidence that downstream allowlisting, DLP, and incident-response controls can act on.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns enterprise-wide discovery and inventory reconciliation for externally hosted AI services, embedded SaaS AI features, browser AI applications, provider APIs, and hosted agent endpoints observed through identity, endpoint, browser, SaaS, proxy, DNS, gateway, and provider telemetry.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-001.004 discovers enterprise users and workloads consuming third-party or externally hosted AI services; AID-M-001.005 discovers the organization's own Internet-reachable AI services from an outside vantage point.
Outbound shadow-AI use and inbound public attack-surface exposure are different populations and must not be combined.

AID-M-001.004 discovers externally hosted AI consumption across enterprise telemetry; AID-M-001.006 discovers organization-owned AI endpoints reachable only through private networks or control planes.
The first follows external service use, while the second enumerates internal service exposure under an explicitly authorized private scope.

implementationGuidance: Ingest AI-service discovery telemetry from identity, network, endpoint, browser, SaaS, and API-gateway logs into a normalized AI service observation schema.
Classify observed AI services against a governed AI service catalog and assign sanctioned, restricted, unknown, or blocked status with technical evidence.
Reconcile discovered AI services with declared AI asset and dependency inventories, then produce drift evidence for downstream controls.

subTechniques.name: Public AI Endpoint & Agent-Service Exposure Discovery
subTechniques.description:
Continuously discover and validate organization-owned, Internet-reachable AI attack surface from an external vantage point: model inference APIs, MCP servers, A2A or Agent Card endpoints, public model or artifact stores, notebooks, Gradio/Streamlit applications, debug or administrative routes, and orphaned test deployments. Classify candidate AI-service evidence before reconciliation, then map confirmed candidates to an owner, environment, approved exposure intent, authentication requirement, optional approved response fingerprint, exception state, severity, and retirement state; unknown or orphaned high-risk services must be brought under management or removed.

Official implementation references: CISA Internet Exposure Reduction guidance at https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/exposure-reduction and the OWASP Secure AI Model Ops Cheat Sheet at https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secure_AI_Model_Ops_Cheat_Sheet.html.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns authorized, credential-free, outside-in discovery and validation of organization-owned Internet-reachable AI endpoints and agent services, followed by ownership, exposure-intent, authentication, exception, and retirement reconciliation.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-001.005 discovers the organization's inbound public AI attack surface; AID-M-001.004 discovers enterprise consumption of externally hosted AI and SaaS capabilities.
An externally observed owned endpoint is not the same asset population as an external service used by employees or workloads.

AID-M-001.005 observes public exposure from outside the trusted network; AID-M-001.006 observes private-network and internal-control-plane exposure from an authorized internal scope.
Public and private discovery may share schemas, but their eligible populations, vantage points, authorization, and exposure claims remain separate.

implementationGuidance: Run authorized outside-in discovery and AI-route validation from a network that does not inherit enterprise trust or credentials.
Reconcile externally observed AI endpoints to declared inventory and fail the exposure gate on unknown, ownerless, expired, or authentication-drift findings.

subTechniques.name: Internal AI Endpoint & Agent-Service Discovery
subTechniques.description: Continuously discover and reconcile organization-owned AI endpoints and agent services reachable only through private networks or control planes, including RFC1918/VPC/VNet services, Kubernetes Services and Ingresses, internal inference APIs, MCP/A2A endpoints, notebooks, model or retrieval gateways, and orphaned development deployments. The eligible population must come from signed IPAM, cloud-organization, Kubernetes-fleet, and asset-inventory exports external to the scanner; scanning arbitrary private address space without explicit authorization is prohibited.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns authorized discovery and reconciliation of organization-owned AI endpoints and agent services reachable only through private networks or internal control planes. It reports exact internal exposure facts but does not authenticate, segment, patch, contain, or evict those services.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-001.006 discovers internally reachable organization-owned AI services; AID-M-001.004 discovers use of externally hosted AI services and SaaS AI features.
Internal service exposure and external service consumption require different telemetry, ownership, and reconciliation populations.

AID-M-001.006 uses authorized private-network and control-plane scope; AID-M-001.005 uses a credential-free outside-in vantage point against public exposure.
A service visible in both paths remains two independently measured exposure claims rather than one merged scan result.

AID-M-001.006 discovers endpoints and services from network and control-plane facts; AID-D-016.001 detects new or rogue agents from runtime agent-graph behavior.
A reachable endpoint is not proof of an active agent node, and an anomalous agent graph can reveal actors that static endpoint discovery misses.

implementationGuidance: Reconcile every authorized private-network and control-plane target through signed scope, scanner, and independent replay evidence.

subTechniques.name: Data & Artifact Versioning
subTechniques.description: Implements systems and processes to version control datasets and model artifacts, treating them with the same rigor as source code. By tracking every version of a data file and linking it to specific code commits, this technique ensures perfect reproducibility, provides an auditable history of changes, and enables rapid rollbacks to a known-good state, which is critical for recovering from data corruption or poisoning incidents.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns immutable version identity, reproducible lineage, and change history for datasets, model artifacts, code, and pipeline inputs so an exact prior state can be reconstructed or selected for rollback.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-002.001 establishes which version exists and how it was derived; AID-M-002.002 verifies that bytes match an expected digest and trusted signature.
Version history provides lineage but not cryptographic authenticity, while a valid signature does not by itself provide reproducible version lineage.

implementationGuidance: Use a dedicated data version control system to track large files alongside Git.
Define the data processing pipeline in a version-controlled manifest to map data flow.
Link specific data versions to training runs in an MLOps platform.

subTechniques.name: Cryptographic Integrity Verification
subTechniques.description: Employs cryptographic hashing and digital signatures to create and verify a tamper-evident chain of custody for macro-scale AI artifacts throughout their lifecycle. Focuses on whole-artifact integrity for datasets, model weights, container images, and manifests to ensure you deploy exactly what you built. This technique provides artifact lifecycle integrity from creation through storage to deployment, with provenance verification to prove authenticity and origin.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns whole-artifact cryptographic digest and signature verification for stored or transferred datasets, models, configurations, and related artifacts, bound to the expected identity and provenance record.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-002.002 proves that artifact bytes match trusted integrity metadata; AID-M-002.001 proves version identity and derivation lineage.
Integrity verification and reproducible version history are complementary but independently evidenced claims.

AID-M-002.002 verifies a complete artifact as one integrity object; AID-H-020.001 signs and verifies individual retrieval chunks so partial knowledge-base content cannot be substituted at query time.
A valid whole-artifact digest does not prove the identity of each runtime-retrieved chunk, and chunk signatures do not replace release-artifact verification.

implementationGuidance: Generate and verify whole-artifact checksums (e.g., SHA-256) for datasets, models, and container images at critical pipeline stages.
Sign single-file artifacts with a pinned signer identity and sign multi-file model bundles with an OpenSSF Model Signing manifest; verify the signer and every signed member before promotion or load.

subTechniques.name: External Dataset Content-Risk Characterization
subTechniques.description: Characterize the security- and privacy-relevant contents of each externally obtained dataset before it is used for training, tuning, evaluation, retrieval, or grounding, including measured sensitive-data presence, secrets, label and feature distributions, malformed records, and policy-defined prohibited content.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns content-risk characterization of an external dataset's actual records, distributions, labels, anomalies, sensitive content, and poisoning indicators before downstream admission decisions.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-002.003 characterizes what risks are present in the dataset contents; AID-H-003.003 decides whether the external dataset and its supplier provenance satisfy the admission policy.
A low-risk content scan does not approve an untrusted supplier, and trusted provenance does not prove that dataset contents are safe.

implementationGuidance: Define a versioned content-risk policy for the dataset class and bind it to the complete immutable input manifest.
Stream every CSV and JSONL manifest member through the content-risk profiler and block promotion on findings or incomplete coverage.
Replay the complete content-risk profile from read-only inputs before promotion.

subTechniques.name: Trust-Tiered Memory/KB Provenance & Write Eligibility Contract
subTechniques.description: Define the provenance, trust-tier, evidence, and namespace metadata contract for agent memory, knowledge-base, and vector-store writes. Each candidate write is assigned an eligibility state such as trusted, probation, or quarantined based on caller identity, source trust, validator output, contradiction checks, and reviewed evidence. The resulting contract records who proposed the write, which evidence was used, which policy produced the trust tier, and which namespace or promotion state downstream controls must consume.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns the signed provenance, trust-tier, write-eligibility, evidence, namespace, and retention contract for memory and knowledge-base records. It classifies what downstream gates may consider but does not execute a read, write, promotion, or deletion.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-002.004 defines whether a memory or knowledge record is eligible for promotion and which evidence must bind it; AID-I-004.004 executes the transactional quarantine-to-trusted promotion.
An eligibility contract is not a successful promotion receipt, and the runtime gate must not invent provenance or trust-tier facts.

AID-M-002.004 defines record-level provenance and write-eligibility facts; AID-H-029.002 enforces whether data use is authorized at a particular lifecycle stage.
A record can be technically eligible for storage yet unauthorized for the current stage, purpose, subject, or processing path.

implementationGuidance: Define a versioned KB or memory write eligibility contract that captures caller identity, payload shape, evidence references, validator output, and downstream enforcement fields.
Use policy-as-code to derive and record a recommended trust tier for each KB or memory write candidate based on evidence, source trust, and validator output.
Define trust-tiered namespace metadata and retrieval eligibility rules with explicit promotion, probation, and quarantine states.
Generate promotion evidence by checking candidate facts against trusted facts before any KB or memory entry is marked trusted.
Record immutable provenance for every KB or memory write candidate and promotion decision, including who proposed it, which evidence was reviewed, and which policy produced the trust tier.
Publish source trust-state degradation evidence when verification failures spike, so Harden controls can perform runtime circuit breaking or fail-closed admission.

subTechniques.name: Hybrid Classical + Post-Quantum Integrity & Provenance for Long-Lived AI Assets
subTechniques.description: Preserve the integrity and provenance of long-lived AI assets—including model weights, datasets, checkpoints, evidence bundles, manifests, and restore artifacts—across years of storage, trust-anchor rotation, algorithm deprecation, and archive/restore cycles. Use an explicit dual-signature transition profile: keep a currently interoperable classical signature and add a separately generated FIPS 204 ML-DSA signature over the exact same canonical provenance statement. A separately signed local verifier policy must pin the exact current statement digest, chain root, allowed profiles, maximum lifetime, artifact and provenance locations, and approved trust anchors; verification must require both statement signatures and traverse the prior-statement digest chain.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns classical-plus-post-quantum provenance and integrity continuity for long-lived AI assets whose trust must survive cryptographic migration, including hybrid signatures, algorithm policy, verification history, and migration evidence.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-002.005 preserves integrity trust across a long-lived classical-to-post-quantum migration; AID-M-002.002 performs ordinary whole-artifact digest and signature verification.
Use the hybrid control only when cryptographic longevity and transition continuity are in scope; it does not replace routine artifact verification.

AID-M-002.005 records and verifies long-lived hybrid provenance continuity; AID-H-003.008 enforces crypto-agile signing and distribution requirements when artifacts are admitted or delivered.
The Model control establishes durable trust evidence, while the Harden control blocks distribution or admission that does not meet the active cryptographic policy.

implementationGuidance: Issue and verify separate classical cosign and ML-DSA signatures over one canonical, expiring provenance statement.
Re-verify and roll long-lived provenance before expiry or trust-policy change, preserving an auditable continuity chain for restore.

subTechniques.name: Model Card & Datasheet Generation
subTechniques.description: Create, validate, sign, and retain version-bound model cards and dataset datasheets that describe intended use, limitations, performance, ethical considerations, provenance, and references to the applicable evaluation and validation records. CI checks document completeness and binding to the exact release artifact before publication. This control documents and binds those records; it does not execute the underlying fairness or safety evaluation.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns generation, completeness validation, signing, release binding, retention, and publication of model cards and dataset datasheets. It documents evaluation claims and links their evidence but does not execute the underlying evaluation.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-003.001 documents safety-boundary conformance results and binds them to the release record; AID-M-007.002 executes the deterministic safety-boundary release gate.
A complete model card is not proof that every governed conformance case passed.

AID-M-003.001 publishes fairness and disparity claims with references to evidence; AID-M-007.003 computes and independently replays the applicable fairness release evaluation.
Documentation may report the result, but it must not become the evaluator or substitute for population-complete fairness evidence.

Create and maintain 'Datasheets for Datasets' to document data provenance, composition, and collection processes.
Integrate documentation generation and validation into a CI/CD pipeline.
Store and version control documentation in a centralized, accessible repository or model registry.
Publish a signed CycloneDX model card bound to the release and to independently owned safety-boundary, fairness, and conformance evidence.

subTechniques.name: General Predictive Performance & Operational Baselining
subTechniques.description: Create signed, version-bound reference artifacts for general predictive and operational behavior under approved normal conditions. Measure task-appropriate predictive quality on a trusted evaluation population, serving latency and throughput under a declared load profile, confidence or score distributions where meaningful, and non-LLM output distributions needed by later drift or anomaly detection.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns trusted reference artifacts for general predictive quality, serving latency and throughput, confidence or score distributions, and non-LLM output distributions under declared normal conditions.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-003.002 baselines general predictive and operational metrics; AID-M-003.005 baselines reconstruction error for a governed image or media domain.
A modality-specific reconstruction distribution should not be folded into a generic model KPI baseline.

techniques.name: Automated Agentic Security Benchmarking
techniques.description:
Integrate standardized security benchmark suites (such as AgentHarm, ToolEmu, R-Judge, AgentDojo, InjecAgent, CyberSecEval, garak, PyRIT, promptfoo, or browser-agent regression harnesses) into the CI/CD pipeline to quantitatively measure an AI agent's resistance to adversarial attacks, safety policy compliance, and tool misuse risks.

Coverage includes:
  • General agentic benchmarks for prompt injection, jailbreaks, unsafe outputs, and unauthorized tool use.
  • Agent-injection benchmarks such as AgentDojo and InjecAgent that exercise tool-augmented workflows rather than static prompt strings alone.
  • Cybersecurity-focused model and agent probes such as CyberSecEval and PyRIT campaign runs.
  • Production-trace-derived grading and replay of de-identified real agent sessions, near-misses, incidents, red-team findings, and externally reported bypasses.
  • Browser-agent-specific prompt injection regression and fuzz testing for hidden DOM/CSS instructions, OCR/PDF-mediated injections, cross-origin read-then-act flows, download and clipboard abuse, and magic-link or session confusion.
  • Release gates that compare benchmark results across builds so prompt, model, tool, and browsing changes cannot silently weaken the agent's security posture.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns repeatable, release-bound adversarial security benchmarking of models and agents across static, adaptive, stateful, tool-using, browser, and production-trace-derived scenarios. It measures security regression but does not define the safety boundary, publish model cards, own forensic logging, or prove universal robustness.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-008 owns adversarial security benchmark campaigns; AID-M-007 owns the authoritative use-case safety boundary and its required conformance dimensions.
Benchmarks test resistance under selected attacks, while the safety boundary defines the release obligations and applicability contract.

AID-M-008 exercises broader adversarial and adaptive attack behavior; AID-M-007.002 proves the complete signed deterministic conformance case population.
A benchmark campaign and a deterministic policy gate answer different questions and neither should be reported as the other.

AID-M-008 measures adversarial security resistance and regression; AID-M-003.007 establishes the signed expected LLM behavior and prompt-suite reference.
A stable golden baseline supports comparison, while adaptive benchmarking deliberately searches beyond expected behavior for bypasses.

techniques.name: Agent Autonomy & Authority Governance
techniques.description:
Define and version the control-plane facts that determine an agent's approved mission, functional autonomy, authority envelope, accountable runtime identity and delegation lineage, live trust state, and required control profile. The child controls partition those dimensions into separate control objectives, while preserving one chain from approved purpose to constrained runtime authority and recoverable change history.

Example: a support agent may read a knowledge base and draft replies autonomously, require approval before sending email, and be forbidden from issuing refunds or changing credentials. Its exact workload identity, delegated scope, goal-manifest digest, authority-envelope version, and current trust state must remain bound to that decision.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns signed governance facts for an agent's functional autonomy, authority envelope, runtime identity and delegation lineage, goal changes, trust state, and required capability-tier control profile. It publishes facts for enforcement but never grants an action solely from a governance artifact.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-009 defines and publishes the approved autonomy, authority, identity, delegation, trust-state, and control-profile facts; AID-H-018 verifies those facts at the runtime action boundary and returns the authorization outcome.
Governance states what authority should exist, while runtime enforcement decides whether the exact current action may proceed.

subTechniques.name: Operating Scope & Functional Autonomy Profiles
subTechniques.description:
Define what kind of autonomy an agent is approved to have before deployment. This sub-technique records the operating scope and the per-function autonomy profile across Observe, Analyze, Decide, Execute, Delegate, and Persist.
Key question: what may this agent do on its own? This gives downstream policy, monitoring, and approvals a clear contract to enforce.
Example: a customer-support agent may Observe and Analyze autonomously, but Execute refunds and Persist long-term customer memory still remain supervised.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns the approved operating scope and per-function autonomy profile across Observe, Analyze, Decide, Execute, Delegate, and Persist. It answers which functions the agent may perform independently or only under supervision.

AID-M-009.001 defines the functional autonomy profile; AID-M-009.006 maps the resulting capability and blast-radius tier to mandatory defensive control evidence.
Autonomy classification is an input to assurance requirements, not proof that those controls are deployed and effective.

subTechniques.name: Authority Envelope & Action Risk Classification
subTechniques.description:
Define the hard authority boundaries around the agent and the risk model used to judge actions inside them. This sub-technique translates a general mission into machine-checkable limits on tools, data classes, environments, effect types, budgets, and delegation depth, then classifies actions by base risk and mandatory adjustment factors.
Key question: is this requested action still inside the approved envelope? This lets policy engines fail closed when the answer is no.
Example: support-agent-prod-001 may use search_kb and create_ticket on support data, but may not call issue_refund, export a full customer table, or delegate to an external billing agent.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns the machine-checkable authority envelope and action-risk classification for tools, data classes, environments, effect types, budgets, and delegation depth. It supplies policy facts but does not itself return the runtime allow or deny decision.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-M-009.002 defines concrete authority limits and action risk inside the mission; AID-M-009.001 defines how independently the agent may Observe, Analyze, Decide, Execute, Delegate, or Persist.
Authority and autonomy are orthogonal: permission to perform an action and permission to perform it without supervision are separate decisions.

AID-M-009.002 defines the approved authority envelope and action-risk facts; AID-H-018.002 evaluates the exact runtime request against active policy and returns the authorization outcome.
A valid envelope is policy input, not a pre-authorized action.

AID-M-009.002 classifies action authority and risk; AID-M-009.006 binds the agent's aggregate capability and blast-radius tier to the required defensive control profile.

Bind autonomous actions to an accountable runtime identity and preserve chain of custody across delegation. This sub-technique covers owner and sponsor registration, workload identity issuance, WIMSE-aligned workload-to-workload identity patterns, short-lived task credentials, RFC 8693 token exchange or provider-native on-behalf-of token minting, signed delegation context, actor identity claims, and the normalized authorization context consumed by a runtime enforcement point.

Identity and delegation evidence are necessary inputs but are not themselves an authorization result.

Key question: what verified trust-state change should downstream enforcement consume when behavior turns risky?

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns the trust-state model, transition rules, signed and freshness-bounded state publication, monotonic transition history, and restoration criteria for Normal, Elevated, Degraded, Restricted, or Quarantined agent states. tactics.name: Harden
tactics.description: The "Harden" tactic encompasses proactive measures taken to reinforce AI systems and reduce their attack surface before an attack occurs. These techniques aim to make AI models, the data they rely on, and the infrastructure they inhabit more resilient to compromise. This involves building security into the design and development phases and applying preventative controls to make successful attacks more difficult, costly, and less impactful for adversaries.

techniques.name: Adversarial Robustness Training
techniques.description: Proactively improve a model's resistance to declared adversarial-input and model-level evasion threats through adversarial examples, robust training objectives, and architecture-specific regularization methods whose benefit is demonstrated by independent replay without unacceptable task-quality loss.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: This technique owns training-time changes that make a model measurably more resistant to declared adversarial-input and model-level evasion threats, including adversarial-example training, robust objectives, and architecture-specific regularization, together with threat-specific pass criteria verified by independent replay. Architecture or representation choices such as relative position bias or rotary positional embeddings do not satisfy this technique unless they are independently shown to improve the declared robustness outcome. It does not own evaluation-data integrity, instruction-hierarchy protection against prompt injection, or runtime authorization of tools and side effects.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-001 changes the model to improve adversarial robustness; AID-H-007.004 protects the evaluation evidence used to substantiate that robustness.
AID-H-007.004 covers the integrity, independence, sufficiency, and promotion use of datasets, holdouts, benchmarks, and test evidence. It applies whether or not adversarial training was used, and AID-H-001 cannot compensate for manipulated or insufficient evaluation evidence.

AID-H-001 targets adversarial examples and model-evasion threats; AID-H-016 protects instruction precedence against prompt injection.
Both can involve model training, but AID-H-016 separates trusted instructions from untrusted data and teaches instruction-following systems to preserve the instruction hierarchy. Neither technique substitutes for the other.

AID-H-001 improves model robustness; AID-H-018 authorizes and constrains runtime tool actions and side effects.
AID-H-001 does not authorize tool calls, constrain parameters, or make side effects transaction-safe. AID-H-018 remains necessary regardless of adversarial-training results.

subTechniques.name: Inference-Time Prompt & Input Validation

subTechniques.name: Dataset Split Integrity, Partition Governance & Leakage Prevention
subTechniques.description: Ensure the integrity and security of dataset partitioning into training, validation, and test splits. Adversarial partitioning, post-hoc split manipulation, and train-test leakage can make a compromised model look better than it is and can invalidate downstream evaluation. This sub-technique enforces deterministic and auditable splitting, split immutability, exact and near-duplicate leakage detection across partitions, representative stratification checks, and access controls so training and evaluation code cannot casually read each other's splits.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns deterministic and auditable train, validation, and test partitioning, split immutability, duplicate and near-duplicate leakage detection, representative stratification, temporal integrity, and split-level access controls.

implementationGuidance: Use deterministic split generation with recorded seed, split metadata, and split artifact hashing so every split can be reproduced and verified later.
Check for exact duplicates and near-duplicates across train, validation, and test before training begins, and block if leakage exceeds defined thresholds.
Apply split-level access control so training jobs can only read the training partition and evaluation jobs can only read the validation or test partitions they need.
Verify that the split remains representative by checking class balance, temporal integrity, and important feature distributions across partitions.

subTechniques.name: External Media & Document Provenance Verification
subTechniques.description:
Verify provenance metadata for external images, video, PDFs, and documents before they are ingested into multimodal RAG, OCR, evidence-processing, OSINT, or agent workflows. This sub-technique focuses on inbound provenance verification, not outbound watermarking.

Coverage includes:
  • Verifying C2PA / Content Credentials where available.
  • Classifying inputs as verified, unsigned, invalid, or stripped.
  • Preserving provenance state through OCR, chunking, embedding, and downstream retrieval metadata.
  • Requiring step-up review when high-impact workflows rely on unsigned or invalid media.
Critical processing order: when this control is paired with multimodal sanitization, provenance extraction and verification must occur before any strip-all-metadata or media-rebuild step. Verify and preserve the C2PA / Content Credentials verdict first, then allow downstream sanitization to strip non-provenance metadata or rebuild media bytes as required.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns inbound cryptographic provenance verification for externally produced media and documents before OCR, chunking, embedding, or sanitization, and propagates the verified, unsigned, invalid, or stripped state into downstream metadata.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-002.007 verifies source attestation before destructive normalization; AID-H-002.003 strips unsafe metadata, decodes, rebuilds, and admits the artifact.
The provenance verdict must be preserved before sanitization changes the original bytes or metadata.

AID-H-002.007 verifies an external publisher or capture-device attestation chain; AID-D-001.002 uses signal-level forensics to detect synthetic or manipulated media.
Cryptographic provenance and forensic authenticity are independent verdicts and either may be absent or contradictory.

AID-H-002.007 verifies third-party media provenance at inbound use; AID-M-002.002 verifies whole-artifact integrity against organization-governed digests and signatures.
External publisher trust and internal artifact-lifecycle trust use different authorities and populations.

AID-H-002.007 establishes the source-media provenance verdict before OCR and chunking; AID-H-020.001 protects the integrity of the resulting chunks from ingestion through retrieval.
Source provenance precedes chunk integrity and neither substitutes for the other.

implementationGuidance: Verify C2PA or equivalent provenance metadata at ingestion time and classify each asset as verified, unsigned, invalid, or stripped before it enters OCR, chunking, or embedding pipelines.
Propagate provenance state into downstream chunk, embedding, and retrieval metadata and require step-up review when high-impact decisions rely on unsigned or invalid media.

subTechniques.name: Software Dependency & Package Security
subTechniques.description: At final dependency and package admission in the build or deployment pipeline, verify the complete population of exact resolved package identities, versions, sources, digests, signatures or attestations, SBOM entries, vulnerabilities, yanked status, and license decisions; block when any required artifact or check is missing, stale, unsupported, or fails.

subTechniques.name: Model SBOM & Provenance Attestation
subTechniques.description:
Produce a model-centric SBOM that inventories model bytes (files, hashes), tokenizer, config, format, and loader code commit; bind it to the exact artifact digest via in-toto/SLSA attestation signed with Sigstore.

Interoperability: keep one internal canonical manifest for enforcement, then export standards-compatible AI-BOM formats such as CycloneDX ML-BOM 1.7 and SPDX 3 AI Profile for procurement, regulator, partner exchange, and technical-documentation evidence such as EU AI Act Annex IV-style model and data documentation.

Admission control: verify the attestation and digest binding before promotion, and re-verify hashes at runtime before loading. This creates a tamper-evident content contract for the model, closing name/namespace trust gaps.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns a signed model SBOM and provenance attestation bound to the exact model artifact, including components, training inputs, code, frameworks, adapters, build identity, and lineage needed by release admission.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-003.006 attests the composition and provenance of one exact model release artifact; AID-M-001.002 maintains the broader system dependency map and deployed release composition.
A model SBOM is one artifact-level evidence object, not the complete service and trust-boundary dependency graph.

AID-H-003.006 produces the signed composition and provenance evidence; AID-H-003.002 verifies that evidence and decides whether the release may be promoted and distributed.
Attestation authorship must remain distinguishable from gate enforcement.

AID-H-003.006 describes the complete model release and its components; AID-H-003.007 applies adapter and PEFT-specific identity, base-model binding, provenance, and compatibility admission.
An adapter can have an independent supply chain even when listed in the model SBOM.

implementationGuidance: Create deterministic model package and compute digest
Generate Model SBOM (JSON) describing bytes and critical metadata
Export AI-BOM evidence in interoperable formats such as CycloneDX ML-BOM 1.7 and SPDX 3 AI Profile while keeping the enforcement manifest canonical.
Sign the artifact-bound SBOM attestation and the canonical SBOM under one pinned Sigstore release identity.
Publish as OCI artifact with digest addressing (optional but recommended)
Admit only an immutable model artifact whose SBOM signature, attestation predicate, signer identity, and actual digest all verify.
Re-verify both Sigstore bundles and the actual model digest immediately before every model load or hot reload.
Deny model refresh, transfer, promotion, deployment, or reload when a verified upstream namespace/owner tombstone applies.
Enforce a signed model-format and loader policy; verify exception verdict signatures and recompute the actual artifact digest.

subTechniques.name: Adapter / PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning) Supply Chain Integrity & Provenance Verification
subTechniques.description: Verify the integrity, provenance, compatibility, and release policy of adapter-based model extensions such as LoRA, QLoRA, and other PEFT artifacts before they are loaded, attached, merged, promoted, or hot-swapped into runtime systems. This sub-technique focuses on preventing trojaned, tampered, incompatible, or untrusted adapters from altering base model behavior through cryptographic verification, publisher/source attestation, strict binding to the intended base model and runtime, registry allowlisting, and post-load behavioral validation.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns supply-chain integrity and provenance verification for adapters, LoRA and PEFT artifacts, including immutable identity, source, signature, base-model binding, configuration, compatibility, and loader constraints before composition.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-003.007 admits an adapter and proves its exact base-model and configuration binding; AID-H-003.006 attests the composition and provenance of the complete model release.
Adapter-specific admission precedes and feeds the release SBOM rather than disappearing into it.

AID-H-003.007 verifies adapter source, identity, signature, and compatibility; AID-H-003.009 scans model and adapter files for unsafe serialization and malware.
Provenance does not prove safe loader behavior, and a clean static scan does not establish trusted origin.

implementationGuidance: Require cryptographic verification and provenance attestation for every adapter artifact before load, attach, merge, or promotion.
Bind each adapter to an approved base-model digest, tokenizer/version, target modules, and runtime compatibility manifest; fail closed on mismatch.
Enforce internal registry allowlisting, revocation/tombstone handling, and publisher trust policy for adapters sourced from external hubs or marketplaces.
Run pre-promotion behavioral validation on the adapter-composed model using golden tasks, safety canaries, and regression checks to detect trojans or severe behavior drift.

subTechniques.name: Crypto-Agile Artifact Signing & Distribution (PQC-Ready)
subTechniques.description: Design AI artifact signing and distribution workflows so they can change cryptographic algorithms, verifier policy, and signature requirements over time without breaking release governance. The active build-to-distribution path for models, checkpoints, adapters, containers, manifests, and attestations should support algorithm agility, staged dual-sign or hybrid-sign migration, and verifier-policy updates before promotion or consumption.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns cryptographic agility in the active build-to-distribution path, including algorithm migration, dual-sign periods, verifier-policy evolution, and preservation of required signature sets across redistribution. It does not define release acceptance semantics or archive-lifetime trust continuity.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-003.008 governs how signing algorithms and verifier requirements evolve; AID-H-003.002 defines and enforces the artifact promotion gate under the active approved policy.
Changing cryptography must not silently change release acceptance criteria.

AID-H-003.008 protects active build and distribution during cryptographic migration; AID-M-002.005 preserves classical-plus-post-quantum trust continuity across years of archival storage, rollover, and restore.
Operational distribution agility and long-lived archive provenance have different timelines and verification chains.

AID-H-003.008 governs the signature infrastructure and verifier policy; AID-H-003.006 governs the model SBOM and provenance content bound to the artifact.
Crypto agility changes how evidence is signed, not what composition facts the attestation must contain.

implementationGuidance: Version signing policy separately from the artifact so verifier requirements can evolve without rebuilding the entire workflow.
Use staged dual-sign or hybrid-sign promotion during migration periods and reject artifacts that lose required signatures in transit or redistribution.

subTechniques.name: Model Artifact Static Malware & Unsafe-Serialization Scanning
subTechniques.description: Statically scan model artifacts, checkpoints, adapters, and packaged model bundles before they are imported, mirrored, loaded, promoted, or deployed. The control inspects serialized model bytes and archive members for unsafe deserialization primitives, dangerous pickle globals, embedded code, custom loader requirements, unexpected scripts, and model-format policy violations without executing the artifact.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns format-aware static malware, unsafe-serialization, archive, and loader-hazard scanning of model artifacts before any model loader executes them. Its clean verdict is admission evidence, not proof of safe execution.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-003.009 scans model artifact formats and serialized objects; AID-H-003.001 evaluates third-party software dependencies and packages.
Model-file loader hazards require dedicated format semantics beyond package SCA.

AID-H-003.009 determines whether the artifact contains known unsafe serialization or malware indicators; AID-H-003.006 verifies the artifact's declared composition and provenance.
A trusted attestation does not make unsafe bytes executable, and a clean scan does not establish provenance.

AID-H-003.009 performs static analysis before any loader runs; AID-I-001.005 detonates and observes first load inside an isolated sandbox.
Dynamic loading can reveal behavior that static scanners miss, while sandbox execution must not replace pre-load rejection.

AID-H-003.009 analyzes serialized model and adapter artifacts; AID-H-025.001 analyzes generated code and execution requests for dangerous constructs.
Both are pre-execution gates, but they operate on different artifact languages and loaders.

implementationGuidance: Run static model-file scanners before any model import, mirror promotion, registry acceptance, or deployment, and produce a signed admission verdict that release gates can consume.

subTechniques.name: Deployed AI Software Vulnerability Remediation Lifecycle
subTechniques.description: Continuously identify and remediate known vulnerabilities in deployed AI software components, including inference servers, orchestration frameworks, agent and MCP runtimes or SDKs, plugins, containers, and supporting libraries after initial admission. Maintain a versioned deployed-component inventory, ecosystem-specific advisory coverage, policy-defined remediation deadlines, rebuild-and-redeploy updates, staged rollout and rollback, and time-bound compensating controls when a compatible fix is unavailable. Close a finding only after independent fleet readback proves the affected population is remediated or an approved exception remains effective.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns continuous vulnerability discovery, prioritization, remediation decisions, compatible rebuild or replacement, staged deployment, rollback, compensating-control expiry, and complete-fleet verification for deployed AI software after initial build or deployment admission.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-003.010 continuously remediates vulnerabilities disclosed in deployed software; AID-H-003.001 decides whether exact dependency bytes may enter a build or deployment.
Admission is a point-in-time gate, while remediation maintains the approved posture throughout operation.

AID-H-003.010 owns the need, deadline, staged rollout, rollback, and fleet closure for a software remediation; AID-H-003.002 owns final promotion, signing, and distribution of an approved release artifact.
A remediation normally uses the release gate, but passing that gate does not prove the vulnerable deployed population was replaced.

AID-H-003.010 covers AI application, framework, runtime, SDK, plugin, container, and library software; AID-H-009.002 covers accelerator firmware and drivers.
The inventories, compatibility constraints, rollout mechanisms, and recovery evidence differ even when one change requires coordinated testing with the other.

AID-H-003.010 decides whether deployed software must be upgraded, rebuilt, replaced, disabled, or temporarily isolated and verifies fleet completion; AID-H-028.006 verifies MCP client, plugin, and update authenticity and integrity.
Update authenticity answers whether bytes are trusted, not whether remediation is timely, compatible, complete, or still required.

implementationGuidance: Continuously reconcile the exact deployed AI software population with versioned ecosystem advisories and issue signed, deadline-bound remediation decisions.
Rebuild and redeploy fixed AI software through a drained canary and staged fleet rollout, with rollback and digest-level completion readback.
Use expiring compensating controls when no compatible fix exists, and keep the vulnerability open until replacement or independently verified remediation.

subTechniques.name: Secure Agent-to-Agent Communication
subTechniques.description: Secure the live request path between agents in custom, MCP-adjacent, and standards-based Agent2Agent (A2A) deployments. Each receiver verifies the authenticated peer, protocol version, payload integrity, replay state, task/context ownership, valid task transition, stream order, push-callback authenticity, and per-request authorization before exposing task data or accepting work.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns receiver-side security for live agent-to-agent requests and streams, including peer authentication, protocol and payload integrity, replay state, task and context ownership, state transitions, stream order, callback authenticity, and per-request authorization.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-004.003 enforces the A2A message and task lifecycle after peer identity is established; AID-H-004.002 authenticates the underlying workload, service, or API caller.
Machine authentication does not validate message replay, task state, protocol binding, or delegation context.

AID-H-004.003 secures the selected live peer communication path; AID-H-004.004 verifies discovery records, Agent Cards, endpoint selection, and advertised capability provenance before that path is chosen.
Discovery trust precedes communication enforcement but does not replace it.

AID-H-004.003 validates each receiver-side message and task transition; AID-H-017.006 constrains the end-to-end delegation graph, hop and loop bounds, and capability attenuation across multiple agents.
Per-hop transport security and whole-chain delegation safety are separate controls.

AID-H-004.003 rejects replayed or misbound agent messages; AID-H-018.008 prevents duplicate external side effects from retries, redelivery, resume, and uncertain outcomes.
Message replay resistance does not guarantee that a provider effect executes at most once.

AID-H-004.003 owns A2A peer, task and context ownership, state-transition, stream-order, callback, and per-request authorization semantics; AID-H-004.005 owns the generic end-to-end message envelope and replay primitive across applicable trust boundaries.
The A2A control remains independently implementable and must not be reduced to a reference to the generic primitive.

implementationGuidance: Issue unique, cryptographically verifiable identities to each AI agent (e.g., using SPIFFE/SPIRE).
Enforce A2A v1 task/context authorization, terminal-state immutability, specification-defined stream shape, and authenticated push delivery at the receiving boundary.
Encrypt all agent-to-agent communication channels (prefer mTLS).
Digitally sign each canonical inter-agent envelope for end-to-end integrity, auditable attribution, and replay-resistant receiver verification.
Bind every signed inter-agent message to a unique message ID/nonce, audience, and policy-derived validity window, then reject replay atomically.
Implement identity-preserving protocol translation (anti-scrubbing) for adapters/gateways.
Bind every cross-agent request to delegation context and authorize it at the receiving agent before any side effect.
Pin the A2A v1.0 service parameter and validate each binding-specific request against a digest-pinned official contract before dispatch.

subTechniques.name: End-to-End Message Integrity, Freshness & Replay Protection
subTechniques.description:
Protect security-relevant AI messages end to end when transport security cannot preserve one authenticated channel from the original sender to the final consumer.

Applicability: Use a deterministic signed envelope and atomic replay rejection for paths with terminating gateways or proxies, multi-hop TLS, queues or event buses, store-and-forward delivery, asynchronous webhooks or callbacks, cross-tenant or administrative boundaries, security-critical commands, or TLS 0-RTT and retry exposure. Bind the sender, audience, operation, target, exact content bytes, validity window, unique message ID, and, when required, the originating request.

Not applicable: Only when complete signed path inventory and independent topology readback prove that none of these conditions exists; mTLS alone is not sufficient evidence.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns the conditional, protocol-independent end-to-end envelope profile for exact message-byte integrity, sender and audience binding, operation and target binding, policy-defined freshness, atomic single-use replay state, key rotation, and conditional request-response binding across AI communication paths whose transport is insufficient.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-004.005 authenticates and freshness-binds a message across intermediaries; AID-H-004.002 authenticates the workload, service, API caller, and protected channel.
Transport or caller authentication is necessary but may end at a proxy, queue, or session boundary before the message reaches its final consumer.

AID-H-004.005 provides the generic end-to-end envelope integrity and replay primitive; AID-H-004.003 owns A2A peer, task/context ownership, state transition, stream order, callback, and per-request authorization semantics.
A2A deployments retain their protocol-native checks and add this primitive only on applicable message paths.

AID-H-004.005 atomically rejects an altered, stale, or reused message envelope; AID-H-018.008 prevents duplicate external side effects across retries, redelivery, and ambiguous outcomes.
Single-use message acceptance does not guarantee exactly-once provider behavior, and an idempotency key does not prove message authenticity.

AID-H-004.005 owns a generic envelope profile across untrusted or asynchronous intermediaries; AID-H-034 owns MCP-specific transport, OAuth, routing, handles, Tasks, subscriptions, operation budgets, idempotency boundaries, and disable-state enforcement.
MCP-specific nonce, proof-of-possession, handle, task, or commit-fence mechanisms remain with their MCP controls and do not replace an applicable end-to-end envelope.

implementationGuidance: Define one deterministic signed-message profile that binds exact content bytes to sender, audience, operation, target, freshness, unique message ID, and conditional request context.
Consume each verified message ID atomically before protected processing and retain replay state for the policy-defined acceptance window.
Inventory every AI message path and require the end-to-end profile only where topology, delivery, trust, or security-critical semantics make transport protection insufficient.

subTechniques.name: Evaluation Data Integrity, Sufficiency Assurance & Promotion Governance
subTechniques.description:
Ensure the integrity, independence, and sufficiency of evaluation artifacts used in validation and promotion decisions. This includes evaluation datasets, holdout sets, benchmarks, safety test suites, and security regression corpora.

What this covers: Existing techniques already address training environment security, reproducibility, detector-specific evaluation, and benchmark execution, but this sub-technique provides a general-purpose evaluation security discipline that applies across model types and promotion workflows.

Threat model: The threat model is simple but high impact: if an attacker can manipulate evaluation data or evaluation evidence, a compromised model can appear to pass all validation gates and be promoted as if it were safe.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns integrity, independence, sufficiency, freshness, leakage checks, and release binding for evaluation datasets, holdouts, benchmarks, safety suites, regression corpora, raw results, and promotion evidence. AID-H-007.004 protects cases, datasets, corpus coverage, and result binding; AID-H-007.007 protects the judge model, grader code, rubric, harness, thresholds, and evidence writer that interpret captured behavior.
Trusted cases can still be mis-scored by a compromised evaluator.

AID-H-007.004 secures benchmark data, independence, sufficiency, and evidence; AID-M-008 executes adversarial agent security benchmark campaigns.
Benchmark execution does not own the integrity of its holdout and promotion evidence.

implementationGuidance: Verify the integrity of evaluation datasets and holdout sets on every evaluation run using content hashes and signed metadata.
Separate training and evaluation storage, credentials, and write paths.

Create signed promotion evidence that binds evaluation results to the exact model artifact, evaluation data version, code version, and configuration used during the run.

Track benchmark freshness and coverage so promotion does not depend on stale or incomplete evaluation suites.

subTechniques.name: Secure Aggregation Protocols for Federated Learning
subTechniques.description: Employs cryptographic methods in Federated Learning (FL) to protect the privacy of individual client contributions, such as model updates or gradients.  These protocols are designed so the central server can compute the aggregate (sum or average) of all client updates but cannot inspect or reverse-engineer any individual contribution.  This hardens the FL process against inference attacks by the server and preserves user privacy in collaborative learning environments.

techniques.name: Classifier-Free Guidance Hardening
techniques.description:
A set of techniques focused on hardening the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) mechanism in diffusion models.

What CFG does: CFG is a core component that steers image generation towards a text prompt, but adversaries can exploit high guidance scale values to force the model to generate harmful, unsafe, or out-of-distribution content.

The threat: High CFG scales can overpower built-in safety conditioning and negative prompts, effectively steering the diffusion model toward disallowed or high-risk generations.

Defense goal: These hardening techniques aim to control the CFG scale and its influence, preventing its misuse while preserving the model's creative capabilities.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns server-side policy enforcement and effective readback for Classifier-Free Guidance and related diffusion guider parameters when untrusted callers can influence them. It does not treat CFG, negative prompts, or risk heuristics as authoritative content filters.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-010 enforces diffusion-specific CFG and guider control surfaces at sampling time; AID-H-002.002 validates general inference prompts and request inputs.
A prompt that passes admission can still request an unsafe guidance configuration.

AID-H-010 owns CFG-specific diffusion semantics and safety constraints; AID-H-033.006 resolves and enforces the complete effective invocation configuration after gateway defaults, aliases, provider translation, and retries.
The gateway must preserve the specialized CFG policy but does not redefine it.

techniques.name: Reinforcement Learning (RL) Reward Hacking Prevention
techniques.description: Design and implement safeguards to prevent Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents and LLM post-training pipelines from discovering and exploiting flaws in reward functions, learned reward models, AI judges, or programmatic verifiers to achieve high rewards for unintended or harmful behaviors ('reward hacking'). This includes classical environment rewards, RLHF/RLAIF reward models, RLVR verifiers, reward-channel integrity, and independent evidence that policies remain aligned with intended outcomes rather than numeric reward maximization alone.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns preventive reward design, learned reward calibration, isolated behavioral promotion validation, reward-channel integrity, and judge or verifier gaming controls for RL, RLHF, RLAIF, RLVR, and related post-training systems.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-012 designs and gates reward systems to prevent exploitable optimization; AID-D-013 detects reward hacking, reward tampering, verifier gaming, and policy manipulation from observed evidence.
Preventive reward controls and production or training detection remain distinct.

subTechniques.name: Robust Reward Function Engineering
subTechniques.description: Directly engineer the reward function to be less exploitable. Define multiple positive goals, explicit negative penalties, and any optional shaping terms as one reviewed reward contract so that the agent cannot get a high score by doing something misaligned, unsafe, or trivial. Potential-based reward shaping is treated here as a reward-engineering method, not a separate control objective: it is acceptable only when the potential function, shaping wrapper, base reward, telemetry, and shortcut tests are versioned and verified together.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns the explicit programmatic reward contract, including positive objectives, negative penalties, shaping terms, shortcut tests, versioning, and evidence that high reward corresponds to intended behavior.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-012.001 engineers explicit environment or task reward logic; AID-H-012.002 governs a learned reward function derived from preferences or demonstrations.
Programmatic reward design and learned signal calibration have different data and failure modes.

AID-H-012.001 prevents shortcuts in the reward function itself; AID-H-012.005 prevents policies from gaming learned reward models, AI judges, or programmatic verifiers during modern post-training.
A well-specified base reward does not eliminate evaluator-specific optimization exploits.

implementationGuidance: Design the RL reward function as a single shaped objective that combines positive multi-objective goals with explicit penalties for unsafe or forbidden behaviors.
Apply potential-based reward shaping only as a reviewed reward-engineering method with logged base rewards, potential deltas, and shortcut-farming tests.

defendsAgainst.framework: Cisco Integrated AI Security and Safety Framework

subTechniques.name: Learned Reward-Signal Integrity & Calibration
subTechniques.description: Protect training-specific integrity of learned reward functions built from preference pairs or expert demonstrations. Enforce signal-mode configuration, leakage-resistant train and evaluation partitions, reward-model calibration, abstention behavior, source-concentration checks, and adversarial validation.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns integrity and calibration of a learned reward signal derived from preference or demonstration data. It consumes label provenance but does not own the general labeling pipeline or the final policy's reward-gaming gate.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-012.002 trains, calibrates, and validates the learned reward signal; AID-H-002.005 proves provenance and integrity of the preference pairs, labels, or demonstrations supplied to it.
Trusted labels are necessary inputs but do not prove reward-model calibration.

AID-H-012.002 governs the learned reward model as a predictive signal; AID-H-012.005 tests whether the optimizing policy exploits that reward model or verifier.
A calibrated evaluator can still contain shortcuts that a policy discovers under optimization pressure.

implementationGuidance: Train and validate learned reward from provenance-bound preference or demonstration signals using isolated splits, concentration checks, calibration metrics, and adversarial holdouts.

subTechniques.name: Secure Reward Signal Integrity & Transport
subTechniques.description: Protect the integrity and authenticity of the reward signal itself. In many real systems, the reward is computed by an external service (simulation backend, telemetry service, rules arbiter). If an attacker can tamper with that reward in transit, the agent will learn a malicious or useless policy. This subtechnique treats the reward channel like a critical security surface: mutually authenticated transport plus cryptographic signing of the reward payload.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns authenticity, integrity, freshness, and service identity for externally computed reward payloads and their transport before the reward is consumed for learning.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-012.004 protects the reward value from transport or service tampering; AID-H-012.001 determines whether the reward function itself encodes the intended objective.
An authentic reward can still be badly designed, and a sound reward is useless if attackers can alter it in transit.

implementationGuidance: Secure the reward channel using mutual TLS (mTLS) and per-service identities.
Digitally sign the reward payload and verify it inside the agent before using it for learning.

subTechniques.name: Decoupled Plan-Then-Execute Architecture
subTechniques.description: Architect the agent so that all high-level reasoning and task planning happen in a non-side-effecting LLM phase, separate from any code or tool execution. The LLM is restricted to outputting a structured plan (for example JSON with action names and parameters) and never calls tools directly. A deterministic Action Selector or Orchestrator then validates, transforms, and dispatches this plan against explicit safety policies and allowlists before invoking real tools. This combines planning and explanation separation from side-effectful actions, making it harder for hallucinated or injected instructions to directly reach infrastructure or sensitive APIs.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns architectural separation of non-side-effecting LLM planning from deterministic validation, transformation, action selection, and dispatch. The model proposes a typed plan but cannot directly invoke real tools.

relatedTechniques.comparison:

An Action Selector is an architectural enforcement point, not a substitute for the authorization policy family.

implementationGuidance: Implement an 'Action Selector' middleware to gatekeep LLM plans.

subTechniques.name: Intent-Based Dynamic Capability Scoping
subTechniques.description:
Dynamically restrict an agent's tool capabilities per request or session based on the authenticated subject, workload, initial intent, and the exact versioned tool registry enforced by the dispatcher, instead of granting a broad static role allowlist.

subTechniques.name: Value-Level Capability Metadata & Data Flow Sink Enforcement
subTechniques.description:
Enforce data-flow safety for agentic systems by tracking the provenance and sensitivity of runtime values (e.g., tool outputs, RAG chunks, web content) and blocking unsafe transfers into sensitive sinks (e.g., outbound email, external HTTP requests, database writes).

The gap this closes: Even if an attacker cannot change which tool is called, they may still manipulate tool parameters (e.g., recipients, URLs, file targets) to exfiltrate data. This is the critical 'data flow diversion' gap.

How it complements other controls: This sub-technique complements role-based allowlists and parameter schema validation by answering a different question: not only 'Is this parameter well-formed?' but also 'Should this value be allowed to flow to this destination?'.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns runtime provenance and sensitivity metadata for values and blocks unauthorized flows into outbound, write, model-call, retrieval, storage, and other sensitive sinks. It answers whether this value may reach this destination, not merely whether the parameter is well formed.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-018.005 enforces provenance-aware value-to-sink policy; AID-H-018.001 validates parameter type, shape, range, and format.
A structurally valid value can still violate data-use or exfiltration policy.

AID-H-018.005 enforces value flows at agent action and sink boundaries; AID-H-029 governs purpose, consent, retention, lifecycle stage, and authorized use of data across the broader AI lifecycle.
The sink gate consumes data-use policy but does not define the complete lifecycle authorization contract.

implementationGuidance: Application-layer value tagging (taint) plus sensitive-sink checks in the tool dispatcher, backed by a versioned policy engine (OPA) and session-isolated metadata storage.
Network-layer egress filtering (service mesh / firewall) to enforce outbound constraints even if application-layer checks fail, with default-deny posture and centrally managed allowlists.
Enforce prompt-body and model-call sink policies before sensitive runtime values are sent to an LLM or external model provider.

subTechniques.name: Tool Side-Effect Idempotency & Transaction Safety
subTechniques.description: Give every state-changing tool effect a server-minted, immutable operation or business-intent ID that remains stable across authorization refreshes and policy-version changes. Execute it through an atomic action ledger, durable outbox, trusted provider registry, provider idempotency key where supported, and explicit reconciliation or compensation path. This prevents retries, duplicate queue delivery, workflow resume, approval webhook replay, and worker failover from silently repeating payments, messages, deletions, tickets, configuration changes, or other external side effects. Approval and policy versions are authorization evidence for the same operation; they must never create a new effect identity. The achievable guarantee is at-most-once effect plus reconciliation for uncertain outcomes; do not claim distributed exactly-once execution unless the effect and ledger share one transactional resource.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns immutable operation or business-intent identity, atomic action ledger, durable outbox, trusted provider binding, duplicate suppression, at-most-once effect handling, and explicit uncertain-outcome reconciliation or compensation paths for state-changing tools.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-H-018.008 prevents repeated or inconsistent external effects; AID-H-018.006 proves the exact action is freshly authorized immediately before dispatch.
Authorization evidence may refresh without changing the stable operation identity.

AID-H-018.008 designs dispatch-time idempotency and records effect state; AID-R-007 performs post-incident authoritative readback, cancellation, reversal, compensation, and final disposition.
Recovery consumes the ledger but does not redesign the original dispatch guarantee.

AID-H-018.008 prevents duplicate external side effects; AID-H-004.003 protects peer identity, payload integrity, task state, and replay resistance in agent communication.
One message can be accepted once yet still cause duplicate provider effects after retry or worker failure.

AID-H-018.008 suppresses duplicate business effects and reconciles uncertain provider outcomes; AID-H-004.005 rejects duplicate, stale, altered, or context-misbound messages before receiver processing.
An accepted message can still produce an ambiguous external effect, so replay protection does not replace the action ledger.

implementationGuidance: Derive an action key from trusted execution context, reserve it atomically with a durable outbox record, and return the recorded result for duplicate deliveries instead of dispatching again.
Dispatch a reserved action once, propagate the same key to providers that support idempotency, and reconcile unknown outcomes before retrying or compensating.

techniques.name: AI Agent Configuration Integrity & Hardening
techniques.description:
This technique establishes and enforces the integrity and security of an AI agent's instructional configurations (e.g., system prompts, operational parameters, external configuration files like CLAUDE.md).

Defense-in-Depth Strategy: It combines client-side controls to prevent the creation of insecure configurations in development environments, cryptographic verification at runtime to ensure the agent only operates based on a trusted, untampered directive, and context-corpus governance over external runbooks, tool specifications, and operational knowledge so the agent does not act on stale, conflicting, or unauthorized context.

Structured Format Mandate: Crucially, this technique mandates the use of structured, non-executable formats (e.g., schema-validated JSON, YAML) for configurations, prohibiting the use of formats that could be interpreted as executable code.

This directly counters attacks where adversaries manipulate an agent's behavior by injecting malicious instructions through external or modified configuration files.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns shift-left agent configuration controls, runtime signature enforcement, governed external context sources, and separation of the supervised runtime from its oversight and control plane.
