subTechniques.name: Ephemeral Single-Use Sandboxes for Tools
subTechniques.description: Run each high-risk tool invocation in a fresh, single-use sandbox instance and destroy that instance immediately after the invocation completes, fails, or times out. The unique control value is per-invocation freshness and guaranteed teardown: no reused workspace, no inherited filesystem residue, no lingering process, and no persistent foothold for a compromised tool.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns per-invocation sandbox freshness, one-shot execution, deterministic teardown, lease revocation, and evidence that no workspace, process, or residue survived the tool call. It delegates isolation strength and egress-policy definition to their canonical controls.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-001.003 owns the single-use lifecycle; AID-I-001.002 owns the microVM, user-space-kernel, WASM, or OS-level isolation profile.
This control binds an approved profile to one invocation but does not independently establish the strength of that profile.

AID-I-001.003 creates and destroys the one-shot sandbox; AID-I-001.004 defines and independently enforces its outbound network policy.
A teardown receipt does not prove default-deny egress, and an egress policy does not prove that the invocation used a fresh workspace or was destroyed.

AID-I-001.003 provides one-shot execution and teardown for a tool invocation; AID-I-001.005 detonates an artifact across a declared case population and emits attested raw behavioral observations.
Detonation consumes sandbox lifecycle evidence but has a separate artifact-analysis population and output; ordinary ephemeral tool execution is not a behavioral-analysis result.

implementationGuidance: Provision a fresh, single-use sandbox (microVM / gVisor / Kata) for every tool invocation, execute once, then destroy it.
Broker managed agent sandboxes through a lifecycle-controlled interface that enforces one-shot execution, delegated runtime-profile selection, delegated egress-policy binding, and teardown proof.

subTechniques.name: Sandbox Network Egress Restrictions
subTechniques.description: Restrict outbound network destinations for sandboxed executions with default-deny egress policy and narrow allowlists to reduce exfiltration, callback traffic, and lateral movement after code execution.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns named sandbox egress policies, destination allowlists, externally enforced proxies or network controls, and bypass testing for sandboxed execution. AID-I-001.004 owns the reusable sandbox egress-policy object and its external enforcement; AID-H-019.003 owns admission and observation export for a browser runtime.
The browser control binds to this policy but does not redefine the allowlist, proxy enforcement, or network-bypass tests.

implementationGuidance: Enforce default-deny outbound egress allowlists for sandboxed runtimes.
Publish named egress policy references for managed sandboxes and verify that enforcement occurs outside the sandboxed process.

subTechniques.name: Safe Ephemeral Detonation & Attested Raw Observation Reporting
subTechniques.description: Detonate every policy-designated executable artifact, including scripts, binaries, container images, plugins, and model-loader candidates, against a complete versioned case population inside a short-lived deny-by-default microVM or equivalent boundary. The detonation receives no production credentials or host-write path, exposes only policy-declared instrumented egress, and exports only attested raw behavioral observations plus measurement metadata bound to the artifact digest, analyzer image, sandbox profile, execution receipt, case population, and policy version. Unsupported artifacts, missing telemetry, suspected escape, or absent destruction and residue evidence leave the analysis unresolved and must not be treated as evidence that the artifact is benign.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns safe artifact-detonation orchestration, complete case execution, attested raw behavioral observations, anti-analysis findings, and observation metadata. It does not claim that one run proves an artifact benign and does not issue a promotion credential.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-001.005 owns artifact detonation and raw observation completeness; AID-I-001.003 owns single-use sandbox creation, teardown, lease revocation, and residue checks.
Detonation must consume the authenticated destruction and no-residue receipt before closing a case, but it adds a separate analysis population and attested observation result.

AID-I-001.005 emits attested raw dynamic-analysis observations; AID-H-031.003 combines dynamic, static, and provenance evidence to decide artifact promotion.
A detonation finding is evidence for the promotion gate, not the release decision itself.

implementationGuidance: Orchestrate an automated analysis workflow using microVMs for strong isolation.
Define and enforce a strict behavioral security policy within the sandbox.
Generate a signed behavioral-analysis report whose payload and referenced evidence can be replayed against the pinned verifier.
Monitor for anti-analysis and sandbox evasion techniques.

techniques.name: Network Segmentation & Isolation for AI Systems
techniques.description: Implement network segmentation and microsegmentation strategies using firewalls, proxies, private endpoints, and transport layer security to enforce strict communication boundaries for AI systems. This involves isolating internal components (e.g., training vs. inference environments, data stores) to limit lateral movement, and securing connections to external dependencies (e.g., MaaS APIs) to prevent data exfiltration, SSRF, and MitM attacks. The goal is to reduce the blast radius of a compromise by enforcing least-privilege network access both internally and externally.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns network segmentation, microsegmentation, private connectivity, egress mediation, and measured reachability for internal and external AI communication paths, including agent listeners, discovery endpoints, callbacks, brokers, relays, and direct peer routes. It limits which identities and routes can connect but does not establish message identity or authorize message content.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-002 controls network reachability between AI and agent components; AID-H-004.003 authenticates peer identity, protects channel and message integrity, prevents replay, and authorizes the A2A task.
A permitted network path is not proof that a peer message is authentic or authorized, and secure messaging does not replace network segmentation.

subTechniques.name: Internal AI Network Segmentation
subTechniques.description:
Implement network segmentation and microsegmentation strategies to isolate AI systems and their internal components (e.g., training environments, model serving endpoints, data stores, agent control planes) from general corporate networks and other critical IT/OT systems.

Internal Communication Controls
Enforces strict internal communication rules through firewalls, security groups, and network policies to limit lateral movement and reduce the internal blast radius of a compromise.

Agent Backend Isolation
This also isolates high-privilege agent backends (e.g. orchestration layers with access to credentials, vector DBs, or model registries) from lower-trust, user-facing inference frontends, so that a compromised public-facing agent cannot laterally move into data-rich components.

A2A applicability: The measured internal reachability population includes every agent-to-agent gateway or listener, broker topic or queue, direct peer edge, discovery-advertised endpoint, callback, and relay crossing an internal trust-zone boundary. Apply the allow/deny graph to authenticated workload identities and exact peer routes, not only user-facing service ports.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns segmentation and measured reachability among organization-controlled internal AI components, trust zones, environments, agent listeners, broker topics, and peer routes. It does not govern connections to remote third-party, SaaS, or cross-organization services.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-002.001 segments internal organization-controlled networks and components; AID-I-002.002 governs connections from the AI system to external services and cross-organization agent endpoints.
Classify the path by the destination trust and administrative boundary, not merely by whether the endpoint uses a private address or encrypted transport.

implementationGuidance: Host critical AI components on dedicated network segments (VLANs, VPCs).
Apply least privilege to *internal* network communications for AI systems.
Implement microsegmentation (SDN, service mesh, host-based firewalls) for fine-grained internal control.
Separate development/testing environments from production using distinct accounts or projects.
Regularly review and audit internal network segmentation rules.

subTechniques.name: Secure External AI Service Connectivity
subTechniques.description:
Applies strict network path control, transport security, policy mediation, and monitoring specifically to connections originating from the AI system and targeting external services, particularly third-party or Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) foundation model APIs. Aims to prevent data exfiltration, Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks, and abuse of external dependencies. This also prevents prompt-injected agents from exfiltrating secrets or invoking arbitrary external services; they can only call approved upstreams through a governed path.

A2A applicability: The measured external reachability population includes every remote or third-party agent endpoint, Agent Card-derived route, callback, relay, broker bridge, and cross-organization peer connection. Default-deny unknown destinations and independently read back the effective egress and inbound exposure for the complete endpoint population.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns default-deny network path control, transport security, mediation, and effective-reachability verification for external MaaS, SaaS, API, callback, relay, broker-bridge, and cross-organization agent connections. It does not define internal microsegmentation between organization-controlled components.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-002.002 governs external and cross-organization service connectivity; AID-I-002.001 segments internal organization-controlled AI systems and trust zones.
A privately addressed provider route can still be external by ownership and trust boundary, while an Internet-routable organization-owned endpoint may remain part of the internal administrative population.

implementationGuidance: Integrate external MaaS/API endpoints via private network connections.
Enforce strict egress controls using firewalls and proxies with verified DNS/SNI allow-lists.
Implement transport layer security (e.g., mTLS, Certificate Pinning) for critical egress connections.
Utilize API Gateways to mediate external AI service traffic and apply security policies.
Monitor external egress traffic for anomalies and policy violations.

techniques.name: Quarantine & Throttling of AI Interactions
techniques.description:
Contain suspicious AI activity by degrading, rate-limiting, quarantining, or blocking the specific identity, session, tenant, agent instance, resource budget, or high-risk action that is creating risk.

Control families: child controls separate detection-driven quarantine and safe mode, identity/session/API throttling, resource-token-spend budget throttling, and per-action containment before side effects. This split reflects real engineering ownership: SecOps/SOAR, API gateway, platform/FinOps, and agent orchestration teams.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns reversible response-time containment after a detection, policy, health, trust-state, or budget signal crosses a containment threshold. It translates existing findings into bounded quarantine, degradation, rate limiting, budget throttling, or per-action enforcement; it does not compute the signal or perform durable eviction.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-003 applies reversible quarantine, safe mode, throttling, or action containment; AID-E-002 revokes execution leases and terminates confirmed-compromised runtime processes, jobs, pods, and containers.
Use this family for bounded containment while investigation or recovery proceeds, and E-002 when the incident decision requires authoritative live-execution eviction.

AID-I-003 contains a scoped identity, session, tenant, agent, budget, or action; AID-I-005 applies a last-resort system-wide or tenant-wide halt or severe restriction.
A local quarantine or throttle is not proof that the emergency halt propagated across every required execution boundary.

subTechniques.name: Detection-Driven Quarantine & Safe-Mode Downgrade
subTechniques.description:
Convert high-confidence detector findings, health signals, trust-state demotions, or analyst-approved SOAR decisions into bounded quarantine, safe-mode, or hard-containment actions. This sub-technique owns signed finding intake, target resolution, containment playbook execution, degraded-mode state, escalation from soft throttling to hard containment, and post-action verification.

A2A containment: Disable or quarantine the contained agent's peer registrations, discovery advertisements, message routes, delegated leases, and pending cross-agent work so isolation covers inter-agent execution paths as well as user-facing endpoints.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns reversible detection-driven quarantine, safe-mode downgrade, hard-containment playbook execution, target resolution, and post-action verification. It consumes signed findings or decisions and does not compute anomaly scores or perform long-term eviction.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-003.001 applies reversible detection-driven quarantine or safe mode; AID-E-002 terminates confirmed-compromised active execution and revokes execution leases.
Escalate to E-002 when continued runtime existence is no longer acceptable; do not report a quarantine state as process or pod eviction.

AID-I-003.001 contains a resolved target through quarantine or degraded mode; AID-I-005 issues and enforces a last-resort system-wide or tenant-wide halt.
A target-scoped safe mode can be an input to escalation, but it does not satisfy global halt coverage or restart-gate evidence.

implementationGuidance: Automated quarantine based on high-risk behavior alerts (cut access, move to honeypot, disable key/account).
Design AI systems with a 'safe mode' or degraded functionality state.
Utilize SOAR platforms to automate quarantine/throttling actions.
Trip a hallucination or safety circuit breaker into a degraded operating mode when upstream health signals cross containment thresholds.

Escalate from soft throttling to hard containment when budget exhaustion is paired with suspicious signals such as recursive tool loops, repeated retries, anomalous latency growth, or high-confidence abuse detections.

subTechniques.name: Runtime Context Isolation & Hygiene
subTechniques.description: Enforces strict boundaries and hygiene for volatile working memory (RAM/Redis). Prevents cross-session/cross-tenant context bleed, limits the temporal blast radius of prompt injections (via windowing/resets), and prevents resource exhaustion (DoS/cost burn) via size/token ceilings and TTL.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns isolation and hygiene of volatile active context and working memory by session and tenant, including bounded size, token ceilings, TTL, resets, and fail-closed serialization. It does not partition persistent memory, govern phase-specific secret demotion, or validate summary transformations.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-004.001 isolates volatile session working context; AID-I-004.002 partitions persistent vector, RAG, and long-term memory by tenant and trust tier.
A Redis or in-memory session boundary does not establish durable namespace isolation, and persistent partitioning does not enforce active-context size, TTL, or reset hygiene.

AID-I-004.001 separates and limits active context by session or tenant; AID-I-004.007 removes or demotes secrets and privileged intermediate state at verified task-phase transitions within a live session.
General context isolation does not prove that no-longer-needed sensitive values were replaced when the task moved to a new phase.

AID-I-004.001 owns active-context boundaries and hygiene; AID-I-004.008 validates the security integrity of a summarization or compaction transformation.
A bounded context window does not prove that a generated summary preserved constraints, provenance, or secret-removal requirements.

implementationGuidance: Enforce per-session isolation with mandatory TTL, deterministic size/token limits, and fail-closed serialization to prevent cross-tenant bleed and DoS.
Enforce Context Pinning and Instruction Re-injection to prevent eviction and 'Lost in the Middle' degradation

subTechniques.name: Cryptographic Memory Integrity (Signed Write/Verify Read)
subTechniques.description: Establishes an end-to-end integrity loop for persistent memory: a controlled writer issues signed records (content-hash + metadata + key id), and an integrity-first loader verifies signatures and hashes before any content can re-enter agent context. This prevents direct-to-DB poisoning/tampering and forces memory provenance to be verifiable.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns cryptographic integrity of persistent memory records after an authorized write by signing canonical content and metadata and verifying signatures and hashes before readmission to context. It does not decide who may request a protected write or whether the candidate content should be promoted.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-004.003 proves cryptographic integrity after an authorized persistent-memory write; AID-I-004.006 enforces who may write protected file-backed identity and state resources.
A valid signature does not establish write authorization, and OS-level write protection does not prove that an accepted record's content and metadata remained intact.

AID-I-004.003 verifies signed memory integrity; AID-I-004.004 controls transactional promotion from quarantined to trusted memory.
An intact record can still be untrusted or ineligible, while a promotion receipt must bind to integrity evidence rather than replace it.

implementationGuidance: Controlled writer and integrity-first loader: sign canonical metadata at write time, then verify signature and content hash before any record is returned to the agent.

subTechniques.name: Transactional Promotion Gates (Quarantine -> Trusted)
subTechniques.description: Implements a strict state machine and atomic promotion workflow for high-risk memory writes. Items routed into quarantine cannot influence agent behavior until reviewed and promoted. Promotion must be transactional, auditable, and typically re-signed as trusted. Aligns with trust-tiered memory write-gates (e.g., trusted/probation/quarantined).

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns the durable memory state machine and transactional promotion of an exact quarantined write into trusted memory, including review binding, compare-and-swap state transition, re-signing, audit evidence, and idempotent publication. It does not define the upstream eligibility contract or authorize transient peer data to persist automatically.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-004.004 executes the runtime quarantine-to-trusted promotion; AID-M-002.004 defines the write-eligibility, provenance, trust-tier, evidence, and namespace contract consumed by that gate.
A recommended trust tier is not a promotion result, and a promotion gate must not invent eligibility metadata outside the signed contract.

AID-I-004.004 promotes an approved write into durable trusted memory; AID-I-004.009 promotes a bounded peer-message projection only into transient active context as peer-untrusted data.
A peer context-promotion receipt never authorizes persistence, trust-tier elevation, or durable-memory promotion.

AID-I-004.004 decides and records durable trust promotion; AID-I-004.003 signs and verifies persistent-memory content and metadata integrity.
Promotion must consume integrity evidence, but integrity alone does not determine that the record is eligible for trusted use.

implementationGuidance: Promote quarantined memory through a compare-and-swap state machine and idempotent transactional outbox, binding one approved content digest to one controlled-writer receipt without claiming cross-store atomicity.

subTechniques.name: Memory TTL, Staleness Decay & Forced Forgetting
subTechniques.description: Apply policy-defined trust decay, re-validation, downgrade, and deletion to persistent memory so stale records do not remain implicitly trusted. scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns policy-defined trust decay, revalidation, downgrade, retention, deletion, and forced forgetting for persistent memory records and their derived replicas, indexes, summaries, and caches. AID-I-004.005 governs persistent-record TTL, staleness, revalidation, downgrade, and deletion; AID-I-004.001 governs volatile session-context TTL, size, resets, and tenant isolation.

AID-I-004.005 removes or downgrades persistent records because of retention or staleness; AID-I-004.007 demotes secrets and privileged context when a live task changes phase.
Phase transition is not the same event as persistent-record expiry, and one control's cleanup evidence does not satisfy the other.

implementationGuidance: Attach freshness metadata such as creation time, expiry time, last access time, last validation time, and trust tier to every persistent memory record.
Automatically downgrade or quarantine trusted memory that exceeds TTL or staleness thresholds until it is re-validated by policy or human review.
Apply forced forgetting policies for session-scoped, user-preference, or privacy-sensitive memory classes so they are deleted at session end or after defined retention windows.
Propagate deletion and downgrade actions across derived artifacts such as embeddings, summaries, secondary indexes, caches, and replicas instead of deleting only the primary record.

subTechniques.name: Agent Identity & Persistent State File Write Protection
subTechniques.description: Protect high-trust, file-backed agent identity and persistent state, such as logical identity, primary-memory, and agent-configuration resources, from unauthorized writes that could survive skill removal, restart, or redeployment. Enforce OS-level write restrictions, a controlled-writer path, immutable baselines, reviewed diffs, rollback, and tamper evidence against the complete protected-file inventory.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns write authorization and enforcement at protected file-backed agent identity, primary-memory, and configuration surfaces through OS restrictions, a controlled writer, immutable baselines, reviewed diffs, rollback, and tamper evidence. Database-backed and vector-backed memory use the other AID-I-004 controls.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-004.006 controls who may write protected file-backed identity and state; AID-I-004.003 proves cryptographic integrity of persistent-memory records after an authorized write.
Write authorization and post-write integrity are separate claims and require separate enforcement and verification evidence.

AID-I-004.006 enforces the protected file-write boundary; AID-H-018.007 determines whether an installed skill may request that capability under its permission manifest.
A skill permission is an input to the file control, not proof that the exact write was allowed, mediated, or durably recorded.

implementationGuidance: Default-deny writes to protected file-backed identity/state surfaces, and enforce updates through a controlled writer plus OS-level immutability.
Verify baseline integrity of protected logical resources at startup before loading any file-backed identity/state content.
Run diff checks on protected logical resources after skill install / update / uninstall, but only accept changes that originate from approved change context.
Before a protected write, require an mTLS-authenticated signed scanner result and a one-time approval bound to the verified external principal, tenant, resource, action, and exact content digest.
Restore only from a signed, version-addressed known-good snapshot under a trusted retention-protected root, using a one-time rollback approval bound to the verified principal and exact manifest.
Emit structured tamper / write-attempt audit events for every protected-resource modification attempt, and correlate them to ticket, writer, and rollback context.

subTechniques.name: Task-Bounded Context Segmentation & Secret Demotion
subTechniques.description: Segment active context by task phase within a live session. At each verified phase transition, replace raw secrets, privileged intermediate results, temporary credentials, and internal-only instructions with short-lived scoped handles, redacted summaries, or non-retrievable references when the next phase no longer requires the original value. Bind the transition evidence to the task, old and new phase, policy version, affected context fields, and demotion result.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns intra-session task-phase segmentation and demotion of raw secrets, privileged intermediate results, temporary credentials, and internal-only instructions into scoped handles, redacted summaries, or non-retrievable references when the next phase no longer needs them.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-004.007 changes sensitive context at a verified phase transition within one session; AID-I-004.001 isolates and limits the session's volatile context as a whole.
Session isolation does not prove that a secret was demoted when its task need ended, while phase demotion does not establish cross-session or cross-tenant isolation.

AID-I-004.007 demotes sensitive active context because the live task changed phase; AID-I-004.005 expires, downgrades, or deletes persistent records under retention and staleness policy.
The triggers, stores, evidence populations, and cleanup semantics are different even when both reduce retained sensitive state.

AID-I-004.007 decides which context must be removed or demoted at a phase transition; AID-I-004.008 validates the security integrity of the summary or compaction transformation used to represent remaining context.
A valid compaction does not decide phase need, and a phase policy does not prove that a generated summary preserved constraints or removed secrets correctly.

implementationGuidance: Define task phases explicitly and trigger deterministic context pruning or demotion whenever the agent transitions into a new phase.
Store high-sensitivity values outside conversational context and inject only short-lived opaque handles into active memory.
Separate active context into distinct memory lanes so system-only, credential-bearing, and user-visible context cannot freely mix during a live session.

subTechniques.name: Context Summary & Compaction Integrity
subTechniques.description: At each context summarization, compaction, or distillation event, validate the compacted output before it can re-enter active or persistent context. Preserve security-critical constraints and provenance, detect carried-forward poisoned content, prevent raw-secret retention, and bind evidence to the input and output digests, model revision, transformation policy, and verification result. When the verifier cannot run or does not support the input, keep the summary quarantined.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns validation of each context summarization, compaction, or distillation transformation before its output re-enters active or persistent context. It preserves security-critical constraints and provenance, detects carried-forward poison, rejects raw-secret retention, and keeps unsupported or unverifiable summaries quarantined.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-004.008 validates the compression transformation and its output; AID-I-004.001 isolates and limits the surrounding volatile session context.
Context hygiene does not prove summary fidelity or safety, and a valid summary does not establish session or tenant isolation.

AID-I-004.008 checks whether transformed context is safe and faithful; AID-I-004.005 governs persistent-record retention, staleness, downgrade, and deletion.
Compaction is not a retention receipt, and deleting or expiring a record does not validate any summary derived from it.

AID-I-004.008 verifies a summary or compaction output; AID-I-004.007 decides which secrets and privileged intermediate state must be demoted at a task-phase transition.
When summarization implements demotion, both the phase decision and the transformation validation remain independently necessary.

implementationGuidance: Enforce a structured summary schema that requires explicit retention of safety constraints, policy commitments, and source provenance, and reject any compacted output that fails schema validation.
Run a post-compaction consistency check that verifies safety-critical instructions survived the summarization by comparing the compacted output against a pre-registered set of invariants.
Scan every compacted summary for leaked secrets, PII, and raw credentials before the summary is allowed to enter context or persistent storage.

subTechniques.name: Peer-Agent Message Context Quarantine & Promotion
subTechniques.description: Keep every authenticated peer-agent message outside active and persistent model context until the exact received bytes pass transport-admission and content-validation controls and a trusted promotion service emits a single-use, work-scope-bound receipt for a bounded typed projection. Promoted content remains explicitly peer_untrusted data with no instruction, policy, credential, tool, or delegated-authority semantics. Missing, stale, unsupported, partially covered, or unverifiable evidence remains quarantined and is INSUFFICIENT_DATA or ERROR, never PASS.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns transient quarantine and active-context promotion for messages received from peer agents over A2A, custom agent protocols, gateways, relays, or sub-agent runtimes. It applies when a peer-message path exists and a trusted context assembler can enforce typed trust metadata. Promoted content remains peer-untrusted data with no instruction, policy, credential, tool, delegated-authority, or durable-persistence semantics.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-004.009 quarantines and promotes peer-message content into active context; AID-H-004.003 authenticates the peer, protects the channel and message, prevents replay, and authorizes the A2A task.
A transport-admission PASS is required input but does not authorize model-context admission or change peer content into trusted instructions.

AID-I-004.009 owns quarantine state and context admission; AID-H-002.002 validates the received bytes for schema, encoding, size, and prompt-injection risk.
Content validation is a required signed input, while this control decides whether a bounded projection can enter active context and with which trust semantics.

AID-I-004.009 promotes a bounded peer-message projection only into transient active context; AID-I-004.004 promotes an approved write into durable trusted memory.
A context-promotion receipt never authorizes persistence, trusted-memory status, or reuse beyond its bounded work scope.

AID-I-004.009 owns the peer-message quarantine and context-promotion state machine; AID-H-017.007 is an optional dual-LLM analysis mechanism for untrusted content.
The analyzer can supply evidence but does not own quarantine storage, promotion atomicity, trust metadata, or context-assembler enforcement.

implementationGuidance: Write the exact authenticated peer-message bytes to a deny-by-default quarantine and issue a signed, read-back-verified receipt bound to peer identity, task, policy, content population, and expiry.

Promote only a signed, validated, bounded projection through a compare-and-swap state transition, and force the context assembler to preserve peer_untrusted data semantics with zero delegated authority.

techniques.name: Emergency "Kill-Switch" / AI System Halt
techniques.description: Establish and maintain a reliable, rapidly invokable mechanism to immediately halt, disable, or severely restrict the operation of an AI model or autonomous agent if it exhibits confirmed critical malicious behavior, behaves as a rogue agent (acts far outside its intended parameters in a harmful way), or if a severe, ongoing attack is detected and other containment measures are insufficient. This is a last-resort containment measure designed to prevent catastrophic harm or further compromise.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns the authoritative emergency RUN, HALT, or severely restricted operating decision and its verified enforcement at every required inference and agent-loop boundary. It is a last-resort containment mechanism; it does not itself revoke credentials, terminate every runtime object, or delete durable application state.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-005 halts or severely restricts a complete system or tenant under an emergency decision; AID-I-003 applies bounded quarantine, degradation, throttling, or action containment to scoped targets.
Use I-003 when limited reversible containment is sufficient and I-005 when policy requires a last-resort halt with complete propagation and restart-gate evidence.

AID-I-005 publishes and enforces the emergency operating state; AID-E-002 terminates exact active processes, agent runs, execution leases, jobs, pods, and containers.
A HALT decision can block execution gates without proving that every live runtime object was terminated, so E-002 supplies the separate eviction receipt when required.

techniques.name: Federated Client Quarantine & Exclusion
techniques.description: Quarantine and exclude federated-learning clients whose cryptographically bound identities have been suspended or denied by an authoritative incident-response control plane. Enforce the deny decision at enrollment, client selection, update ingestion, training, retraining, and recovery/unlearning boundaries so a blocked participant cannot rejoin under the same identity or continue contributing cached updates.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns authoritative, identity-bound federated-client quarantine decisions, signed deny-state distribution, and exclusion enforcement at enrollment, selection, update ingestion, training, retraining, and recovery. Statistical clustering and reputation may nominate investigation candidates but cannot independently prove malice or authorize durable quarantine.

techniques.name: Client-Side AI Execution Isolation
techniques.description: This technique focuses on containing a compromised or malicious client-side model, preventing it from accessing sensitive data from other browser tabs, local application context, or the operating system. It addresses the security challenges of AI models that execute in untrusted environments like a user's web browser, Electron shell, hybrid mobile app, or native mobile runtime. This assumes the model or model runtime may already be tampered with or coerced (e.g. prompt-injected, modified weights, wrapped with hostile JS). The goal is not to "fix" the model but to strictly confine its blast radius using sandboxing, least capability, and controlled IPC.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns component-level confinement of a client-side AI model or runtime through Web Workers, sandboxed iframes, WASM capabilities, CSP, and minimal native bridges inside browsers, Electron shells, hybrid apps, or mobile runtimes. It does not own browser-agent task lifecycle or browser-managed and desktop-workspace state.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-007 isolates the embedded client-side model or runtime component; AID-I-008 isolates browser-agent and desktop computer-use state by task or trust zone.
Cookies, localStorage, IndexedDB, cache, history, downloads, clipboard, magic links, desktop profiles, and workspace residue belong to I-008 even when the model component is separately confined here.

AID-I-007 confines a model inside an end-user client application; AID-I-001 isolates managed AI execution in containers, sandboxes, or microVMs.
A client-side Worker or iframe boundary is not evidence that a server-side tool or model workload runs in the managed sandbox family.

techniques.name: Task-Scoped Browser & Computer-Use Workspace Isolation for Agents
techniques.description:
Isolate browser and desktop computer-use agents per task or trust zone across browser context, profile, origin, workspace, and OS-automation boundaries. Cover cookies, local storage, IndexedDB, cache, history, downloads, clipboard, screenshots, desktop-session state, and automation permissions so hostile web content or residual authenticated state cannot cross task boundaries.

The children separately own ephemeral context lifecycle, cross-origin read/write segmentation, download and clipboard transfer quarantine, authentication-bearing navigation isolation, and disposable desktop workspaces with action confirmation.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns task- or trust-zone isolation of browser-managed state and disposable desktop computer-use workspaces, including contexts, profiles, origins, cookies, local storage, IndexedDB, cache, history, downloads, clipboard, screenshots, desktop-session state, and automation permissions.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-008 isolates browser-managed and desktop-workspace state around an agent task; AID-I-007 confines the client-side model or model-runtime component itself.
A sandboxed model component does not rotate authenticated browser state, and a fresh browser context does not prove that the embedded model runtime has a minimal capability boundary.

AID-I-008 isolates browser and desktop state after content is admitted to a computer-use workflow; AID-H-019 owns URL admission, safe fetch, content demotion, observation export, and the outer browser process boundary.
Safe content handling does not replace per-task state isolation, and an isolated workspace does not make an untrusted URL or observation safe.

AID-I-008 owns browser-context and desktop-workspace state lifecycle; AID-I-001.003 owns the enclosing single-use sandbox lifecycle and teardown.
A fresh browser profile can run inside a reused process sandbox, and a fresh process sandbox can still inherit browser-managed state unless both controls are enforced.

AID-I-008 isolates browser and desktop automation state; AID-I-004 isolates conversational context, tool traces, peer messages, and persistent agent memory.
Browser storage or clipboard cleanup does not prove model-context hygiene, and clearing agent memory does not remove cookies, downloads, desktop files, or authenticated browser residue.

subTechniques.name: Ephemeral Browser Context Lifecycle & Storage Partitioning
subTechniques.description: Launch a fresh browser context for each task or trust zone, partition all browser-managed state surfaces (cookies, localStorage, IndexedDB, cache, history) by origin and trust set, and destroy the context deterministically when the task ends. This prevents browsing residue, authenticated sessions, and cached resources from leaking across tasks or being reused by unrelated origins.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns per-task or per-trust-zone browser-context creation, browser-managed cookie and storage partitioning, context rotation, and deterministic context teardown. It does not create the outer browser process sandbox or isolate non-browser agent memory.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-008.001 owns BrowserContext and browser-managed state lifecycle inside the runtime; AID-H-019.003 owns admission and launch of the outer browser runtime plus sanitized observation export.
Process isolation, blocked host profiles, and enforced egress do not prove per-task cookie or storage rotation, while a new BrowserContext does not establish the outer sandbox boundary.

AID-I-008.001 makes browser-profile state ephemeral per task or trust zone; AID-H-017.004 makes agent short-term prompt and session state transient and isolated.
The same lifecycle principle applies to different state owners, and neither control's cleanup receipt satisfies the other.

AID-I-008.001 isolates browser-engine state such as cookies, localStorage, IndexedDB, cache, and history; AID-I-004.001 isolates volatile model and agent working context.
Browser storage is not conversational context, and clearing one does not establish cleanup of the other.

implementationGuidance: Create a fresh browser context for every agent task or trust-zone transition, bind it to a task ID, and destroy it deterministically on task completion with residue verification.
Define trust-set boundaries for origins and enforce state clearing or context rotation whenever a task crosses from one trust set to another.

subTechniques.name: Cross-Origin Read/Write Segmentation with Step-Up Confirmation
subTechniques.description: Separate browsing permissions by origin and effect type. Read-only origins may be inspected without authorization, but state-changing actions on sensitive or previously unseen origins must be suspended and bound to exact browser/request observations before execution.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns the browser-specific observation and enforcement adapter for sensitive or cross-origin writes: complete request interception, stable actionable-element observation, exact request and UI binding, suspension, post-approval re-observation, drift-triggered receipt revocation, and resumption of the same request. It does not create a second generic approval service.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-008.002 observes, suspends, rebinds, and resumes the exact browser action; AID-H-018.003 independently validates the high-impact action and issues the canonical approval receipt.
The browser adapter supplies the exact observed binding but must consume the canonical H-018 decision rather than authorizing the action itself.

AID-I-008.002 re-observes browser state and revokes the receipt on browser-specific drift; AID-H-018.006 owns generic execution-time authorization re-verification and anti-TOCTOU policy.
The browser adapter implements domain-specific evidence and suspension without replacing the canonical runtime authorization check.

AID-I-008.002 enforces the browser action gate; AID-D-015 detects missing, mismatched, expired, replayed, or bypassed approval evidence from independent telemetry.
The detector does not authorize or resume a request, and the enforcement adapter does not replace independent bypass monitoring.

implementationGuidance: Intercept the complete task-scoped browser request population and bind each sensitive or cross-origin write to an exact request plus a stable actionable-element observation, consuming the canonical H-018 receipt only after an unchanged re-observation.
Suspend a sensitive browser action, render a trustworthy confirmation card from observed request facts, and hand the exact canonical action to AID-H-018.003 for approval before resuming it.
Externalize browser origin, operation, and effect classification in a signed policy that the request guard loads fail-closed and re-evaluates for every navigation and write.

subTechniques.name: Desktop Computer-Use Workspace Isolation & Action Confirmation
subTechniques.description: Run desktop GUI / OS-level computer-use agents inside disposable, task-scoped workspaces with logged-out defaults, screenshot redaction, independently reviewed screenshot-injection signals, OS automation allowlists, action-bound confirmation, post-action effect readback, and watch-mode kill switches. AID-I-008.004 applies privileged desktop UI observation and invocation; AID-I-008.002 intercepts and binds sensitive browser requests and cross-origin writes.

AID-I-008.004 contains the desktop workspace and its general clipboard boundary; AID-I-008.003 owns browser download and clipboard transfer quarantine and clean-context handoff.

AID-I-008.004 contains general desktop and UI automation; AID-I-008.005 brokers authentication-bearing browser navigation in a dedicated context.

AID-I-008.004 binds and invokes the exact desktop UI action and reads back its effect; AID-H-018.003 independently validates the high-impact action and issues the canonical approval receipt.

AID-I-008.004 adds desktop-specific re-observation and effect evidence; AID-H-018.006 owns generic execution-time authorization re-verification and anti-TOCTOU policy.
Both checks remain necessary when screen state, target identity, or effective authority can change between approval and invocation.

AID-I-008.004 owns OS and desktop workspace containment; AID-H-019 owns URL admission, safe fetch, browser-content demotion, and sanitized observation export.
Safe web-content handling does not constrain local apps, files, screenshots, or accessibility actions outside the browser surface.

subTechniques.name: Magic-Link & Authentication-Bearing Navigation Isolation
subTechniques.description: Isolate magic links, OAuth authorization redirects and callbacks, password-reset, invitation, email-verification, and other authentication-bearing navigation as separate, brokered transitions. A trusted controller—not the model—must resolve each opaque link handle; verify issuer, audience or client, exact redirect, transaction binding, expiry, state and nonce, PKCE where applicable, and one-time replay state; restrict the dedicated context to signed allowlisted origins with no inherited storage, permissions, downloads, or clipboard; return only a scoped session reference; then destroy the context and verify the destruction receipt. Raw URLs, authorization codes, access or refresh tokens, and link secrets must never enter model context, ordinary logs, or evidence.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns brokered isolation of magic links, OAuth redirects and callbacks, password resets, invitations, email verification, and other authentication-bearing navigation in a dedicated context with issuer, audience, redirect, transaction, expiry, state, nonce, PKCE, replay, origin, and destruction checks. Raw links, codes, and tokens must not enter model context.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-I-008.005 brokers authentication-bearing navigation and returns only a scoped session reference; AID-I-008.003 quarantines browser downloads and clipboard transfers.
Treating a magic link as an ordinary download or clipboard item does not protect transaction binding, one-time replay state, redirect trust, or token secrecy.

AID-I-008.005 owns the dedicated authentication-navigation state machine; AID-H-019 owns general URL admission and safe fetch outside authentication transitions.
A URL that passes generic admission still requires brokered authentication checks when it carries or creates authority.

implementationGuidance: Treat magic-link and auth-bearing link flows as approval-required authentication transitions in a dedicated browser context.

tactics.name: Deceive
tactics.description: The "Deceive" tactic involves the strategic use of decoys, misinformation, or the manipulation of an adversary's perception of the AI system and its environment. The objectives are to misdirect attackers away from real assets, mislead them about the system's true vulnerabilities or value, study their attack methodologies in a safe environment, waste their resources, or deter them from attacking altogether.

techniques.name: Honeypot AI Services & Decoy Models/APIs
techniques.description:
Deploy and isolate decoy AI systems such as fake LLM APIs, ML model endpoints serving synthetic or non-sensitive data, or imitation agent services that appear valuable, vulnerable, or legitimate to potential attackers; record every interaction without exposing production data or authority.

Intelligence Collection
These honeypots are instrumented for intensive monitoring to log all interactions, capture attacker TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures), and gather threat intelligence without exposing real production systems or data. They can also be used to slow down attackers or waste their resources.

Operational Requirements
All honeypot services must be logically isolated from production networks, run with read-only/non-destructive behaviors, and be instrumented for forensic retention (full request capture, replayable context).

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns the isolated decoy AI service, its synthetic behavior, and the evidence generated by interactions with that service. It must not expose production data, authority, credentials, or a route to a real inference backend.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-DV-001 operates a complete decoy AI service; AID-DV-006 exposes narrow synthetic reconnaissance routes at a gateway or proxy.
Use AID-DV-001 when the attacker interacts with an imitation model, agent, or API service. Use AID-DV-006 when only selected metadata or diagnostic-looking routes are populated and intercepted upstream.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns passive, pre-seeded honey records, decoy artifacts, fake credentials, and canary tokens placed in datasets, repositories, configuration, or documentation. relatedTechniques.comparison:

techniques.name: Dynamic Response Manipulation for AI Interactions
techniques.description: For a high-confidence malicious session that satisfies a versioned deception-eligibility policy, deliberately return a controlled low-utility, misleading, randomized, or safe-no-op response to frustrate extraction, injection, jailbreak, or tool-misuse attempts and collect additional intelligence.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns deception-response eligibility, bounded execution, telemetry, and deterministic return to the normal allow, block, or review path for a high-confidence malicious session. Never activate it from a single weak signal, for ordinary users, or in excluded policy-defined high-impact domains. It requires calibrated multi-signal eligibility, legal and product approval, internal tagging, bounded duration, explicit exit conditions, and an independently controlled deception-mode disable switch.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-DV-003 selects and serves a controlled deceptive response; AID-H-018 authorizes and constrains actual tool actions and side effects.
A deception response or safe no-op does not replace the canonical runtime authorization policy for a real tool or capability.

AID-DV-003 can disable deception mode; AID-I-005 halts or severely restricts the AI system or tenant.
The deception-mode switch returns traffic to the normal response path and must not be represented as a system-wide emergency halt.

techniques.name: AI Output Telemetry Traps & Leak Beacons
techniques.description:
Telemetry Traps
Design model or agent APIs to return unique, benign marker strings only for tightly controlled trap prompts, trap-only synthetic records, or synthetic probe workflows. A marker hit outside the trusted runtime is treated as evidence of scraping, model theft, unauthorized model replay, or enterprise data leakage.

Leak Beacons
Maintain a private registry of exact marker strings, trap identifiers, activation events, and investigation owners. Continuously scan relevant external surfaces and internal telemetry for exact marker reuse, then correlate hits with the original trap activation and access logs.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns controlled trap prompts, exact benign marker strings, leak beacons, activation telemetry, external marker scanning, and marker-hit investigation. A marker establishes correlation with the registered trap workflow; it does not by itself prove watermark provenance, dataset access, or unauthorized training.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-DV-004 registers and investigates exact deception markers; AID-H-013.001 embeds and verifies watermarks or signed content provenance.
A leak investigation may consume AID-H-013.001 detector results, but this technique does not own watermark embedding, C2PA provenance, or modality-specific watermark registries.

AID-DV-004 activates and tracks output markers; AID-DV-002 owns pre-seeded honey data, decoy artifacts, fake credentials, and access-triggered canary tokens.
Use AID-DV-004 for marker reuse observed after a controlled activation, and AID-DV-002 for interaction with a decoy item that already exists in an asset or repository.

AID-DV-004 investigates externally observed exact marker reuse; AID-DV-007 measures registered behavioral canaries in a controlled training or fine-tuning context.
AID-DV-004 consumes a DV-007 canary only when that canary is deliberately registered for external leak investigation; it does not own the training-run measurement.

techniques.name: Training-Data Provenance & Behavioral Canaries
techniques.description: Insert authorized, synthetic, non-sensitive behavioral canaries into a controlled training or fine-tuning corpus and later run a pre-registered, statistically powered recall audit against the exact model version. The control produces evidence that a measured model exhibits behavior associated with the registered canary set; it does not by itself prove who copied data, when training occurred, or that the surrounding corpus was stolen.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns authorized behavioral-canary design, insertion provenance, blinded measurement against the exact model and query profile, statistical evidence, and handoff. Its result associates measured behavior with the registered canary set; it does not prove who copied data, when training occurred, that the surrounding corpus was stolen, or that a training anomaly is poisoning.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-DV-007 inserts and measures training-specific behavioral canaries; AID-DV-002 owns operational honey records, decoy artifacts, fake credentials, and access-triggered tokens.
AID-DV-002 alerts on interaction with planted material, while this technique requires a registered training insertion and a statistically powered model-behavior audit.

AID-DV-007 produces training-bound behavioral-canary evidence; AID-DV-004 owns external exact-marker observation and leak investigation.
An externally observed marker is handled by AID-DV-004 only when the behavioral canary was deliberately registered for that investigation path.

AID-DV-007 measures registered canary behavior after authorized insertion; AID-H-007.002 monitors the integrity and behavior of the running training job.
Canary loss or gradient signals may support investigation, but training telemetry and poisoning detection do not become a provenance verdict under this technique.

tactics.name: Evict
tactics.description: The "Evict" tactic focuses on the active removal of an adversary's presence from a compromised AI system and the elimination of any malicious artifacts they may have introduced. Once an intrusion or malicious activity has been detected and contained, eviction procedures are executed to ensure the attacker is thoroughly expelled, their access mechanisms are dismantled, and any lingering malicious code, data, or configurations are purged.

techniques.name: Compromised Credential, Session, Principal & Grant Eviction
techniques.description: Evict compromised authentication and authorization objects from effective use after a verified incident by applying authoritative revocation to four non-overlapping populations: root or long-lived credential objects; already-issued tokens, authentication sessions, and leases; AI-agent or workload principals and their ability to obtain new credentials; and delegated grants or connected-app authorizations. Each child owns one object population and authoritative control plane, and evidence for one population does not prove eviction of another.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns authoritative incident-time eviction of four authentication and authorization object populations: root or long-lived credential objects, already-issued tokens and authentication sessions, AI-agent or workload principals and issuance paths, and delegated grants or connected-app authorizations. Evidence for one population does not prove eviction of another.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-E-001 revokes authentication and authorization objects; AID-E-002 terminates active processes, agent runs, execution leases, supervisor jobs, pods, and containers.
Credential or session revocation does not prove that compromised code stopped executing, and process termination does not revoke the identities or artifacts that could start new execution.

AID-E-001 evicts identity-plane credentials, sessions, principals, and grants; AID-E-005 removes durable application and agent state.
Application session records, conversational memory, webhook or tool registrations, queues, and schedules require separate teardown even after authentication objects are revoked.

AID-E-001 invalidates compromised or prior authentication and authorization state; AID-R-003.001 creates a new trusted interactive session after eviction.
Successful reauthentication does not prove that the old credential, token, grant, or session population was revoked, and eviction does not itself establish a recovered session.

subTechniques.name: Root & Long-Lived Credential Object Eviction
subTechniques.description: Revoke, disable, rotate, or invalidate the exact incident-scoped population of root and long-lived credential objects, including passwords, API keys, client secrets, signing keys, and long-lived certificates, at their authoritative issuer or verifier regardless of whether the owning principal is a human, conventional service, AI agent, or workload.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns incident-time revocation, disablement, rotation, or invalidation of the exact root and long-lived credential-object population, including passwords, API keys, client secrets, signing keys, and long-lived certificates. Routine non-incident secret rotation is outside this control.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-E-001.001 evicts root and long-lived credential objects; AID-E-001.002 revokes already-issued tokens, authentication sessions, cookies, certificates, and leases.
Rotating a root secret does not prove that every artifact already issued from it is unusable, so both controls may be required for the same incident.

AID-E-001.001 evicts individual long-lived credentials; AID-E-001.003 disables the AI-agent or workload principal and its ability to obtain new credentials.
A principal can retain other issuance paths after one secret is rotated, while disabling the principal does not independently rotate every exposed credential object.

AID-E-001.001 evicts credential objects; AID-E-001.004 removes delegated grants and connected-app authorizations.
A grant can sustain or recreate access after credential rotation, and grant revocation does not invalidate an unrelated password, key, secret, or certificate.

implementationGuidance: Rotate or invalidate the exact incident-scoped population of root and long-lived secret credential objects across every declared consumer and verifier.
Reset compromised human password credential objects without claiming revocation of issued sessions.
Disable and remove exact attacker-created root or long-lived credential objects.
Rotate compromised issuer signing or trust material only when the issuer credential boundary itself is affected.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns revocation or invalidation of the complete incident-scoped population of already-issued access and refresh tokens, session cookies, authorization-server sessions, gateway authentication sessions, workload certificates, established authenticated channels, and agent-to-agent leases. relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-E-001.002 revokes already-issued authentication artifacts; AID-E-001.001 evicts their root or long-lived credential objects.

subTechniques.name: AI Agent & Workload Principal and Issuance Disablement
subTechniques.description:
Disable the exact compromised AI-agent or workload principal at every authoritative identity, workload, federation, and authorization control plane, and stop that principal from obtaining newly issued credentials or tokens. Applicable principal and issuance objects include agent identities, workload or service-principal records, SPIFFE workload entries, cloud workload-identity bindings, provider-native agent identities, and token-exchange or on-behalf-of issuance permissions.

Eviction sequence:
  1. Disable the principal and stop new issuance or delegated minting.
  2. Deny the principal at every reachable authorization and federation boundary.
  3. Invalidate or deny every applicable fresh-authentication and issuance path.
  4. Register a separately attested replacement principal under least privilege when recovery requires one.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns disablement of the exact compromised AI-agent or workload principal at every authoritative identity, workload, federation, and authorization plane and denial of every fresh credential or token issuance path. A separately attested replacement principal is a recovery object, not proof that the original principal was disabled.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-E-001.003 disables the principal and stops new issuance; AID-E-001.001 revokes or rotates individual root and long-lived credential objects.
Principal disablement does not independently rotate every exposed password, key, secret, signing key, or certificate.

AID-E-001.003 stops the principal from obtaining new authentication artifacts; AID-E-001.002 revokes tokens, sessions, certificates, and leases that were already issued.
An issuer-side disablement does not prove that every relying party rejects previously issued artifacts.

AID-E-001.003 disables an AI-agent or workload principal and its issuance paths; AID-E-001.004 removes delegated grants and connected-app authorizations.
Delegated authorization can remain independently effective or associated with another principal, so its authoritative grant population requires separate eviction.

implementationGuidance: Disable every exact SPIFFE/SPIRE workload registration entry for the compromised principal and prove fresh SVID issuance is denied.
Use the prebuilt token-exchange deny-bundle control to block compromised agent actors and verify fresh downstream token minting fails.
Disable the compromised cloud workload-identity binding and prove fresh credential minting is denied.
Disable and, when authorized, remove exact attacker-created AI-agent or workload principal objects.
Reconcile every applicable identity-plane disablement target against authoritative principal, issuance, federation, and authorization state.

subTechniques.name: Delegated Grant & Connected-App Authorization Revocation
subTechniques.description: Revoke the complete incident-scoped population of delegated OAuth grants, connected-app consents, service-principal app-role assignments, token-exchange or on-behalf-of delegated authorizations, and SaaS application grants that can mint fresh tokens or sustain access after ordinary token invalidation.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns incident-time revocation of delegated OAuth grants, connected-app consents, app-role assignments, token-exchange or on-behalf-of authorizations, and SaaS application grants that can mint fresh tokens or sustain access. It does not own credential, token, principal, application-state, or pre-incident authorization design.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-E-001.004 removes delegated authorization objects; AID-E-001.001 evicts root and long-lived credentials.
Grant revocation does not rotate an exposed password, key, client secret, signing key, or certificate, and credential rotation does not necessarily remove an independent connected-app consent.

AID-E-001.004 removes authorization that can sustain or recreate access; AID-E-001.002 revokes tokens and authentication sessions already issued under that authority.
Both controls are required when issued artifacts remain valid after the underlying grant is removed.

AID-E-001.004 revokes delegated grants and app authorizations; AID-E-001.003 disables the compromised AI-agent or workload principal and stops new principal issuance.
Removing one grant does not disable the principal's other authorization paths, while principal disablement does not prove removal of every connected-app or delegated grant object.

AID-E-001.004 performs incident-time removal of delegated grant objects; AID-H-034.002 enforces MCP server OAuth resource boundaries and delegation safety before compromise.
Preventive OAuth design does not revoke a compromised live grant, and grant eviction does not replace correct protected-resource and audience enforcement.

AID-E-001.004 removes authorization grants; AID-E-005 deletes rogue webhook, tool-registration, queue, schedule, and durable application-state records.
Revoke the grant before or alongside teardown, but do not treat removal of either population as proof that the other is gone.

implementationGuidance: Enumerate delegated OAuth grants, connected apps, app-role assignments, and SaaS consents tied to the compromised principal or agent.
Revoke delegated OAuth grants, connected-app consents, token-exchange or on-behalf-of authorizations, and app-role assignments that allow continued access after compromise.
Verify grant-revocation propagation and monitor for attempted reuse of revoked connected-app access.

techniques.name: AI Runtime Process, Lease & Pod Eviction
techniques.description: Revoke compromised execution leases and terminate confirmed-compromised AI model processes, agent runs, supervisor jobs, pods, or containerized runtime instances so active malicious execution stops and cannot reacquire work.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns revocation of active execution leases and termination of confirmed-compromised processes, agent runs, supervisor jobs, pods, containers, and run-local ephemeral execution. It does not remove the credentials, durable application state, or deployable artifacts that could recreate execution.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-E-002 terminates active execution; AID-E-001 revokes the credentials, sessions, principals, and grants that authorize execution.
A killed process can restart while authority remains, and revoked authority does not prove that the currently running workload stopped.

AID-E-002 terminates active workers, processes, runs, jobs, pods, and containers; AID-E-005 removes durable application session, memory, registration, queue, and schedule records.
Runtime termination does not delete durable records that can relaunch work, while deleting a queued or scheduled record does not terminate work that is already executing.

AID-E-002 stops live execution instances; AID-E-003 quarantines or evicts malicious model, dataset, adapter, code, and configuration artifacts.
A terminated workload may be recreated from the same malicious artifact, and artifact eviction does not itself stop an already running in-memory process.

techniques.description: After an incident decision binds confirmed or policy-mandated malicious artifacts to exact immutable identities, quarantine or evict those artifacts and route non-detachable model impact to the canonical recovery owner. Apply only manifest-authorized removal or isolation, create durable tombstones, and make the complete affected artifact population ineligible for serving.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns manifest-authorized quarantine or eviction of confirmed malicious model, dataset, graph, adapter, code, and configuration artifacts; durable tombstone propagation; serving ineligibility; and routing of non-detachable model impact to recovery. AID-E-003 removes or quarantines malicious artifacts; AID-E-002 terminates active execution processes, leases, jobs, pods, and containers.

Eviction does not establish recovered-model readiness, and successful model recovery does not prove removal of every compromised artifact or derivative.

techniques.name: Incident Exploit-Path Closure Verification
techniques.description: After applicable eviction is complete and the canonical Harden or Restore owner has produced signed fix evidence, independently verify that the exact exploited path is closed across the complete incident-defined affected population. Bind the population to immutable asset, workload, service, release, fix-artifact, and policy identities; read back effective versions, configurations, policies, routes, and enforcement state using a separately credentialed verifier; then replay the exact exploit plus policy-defined negative, bypass, stale-state, and partial-rollout cases from an independent vantage point. Accept closure only when every applicable affected target consumes the exact approved fix and every required replay shows that the exploited path can no longer reach the protected effect. An omitted target, missing or unverifiable fix receipt, unavailable readback, incomplete replay population, verifier error, deployment-tool success response, or owner assertion cannot establish closure.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns independent incident-scoped verification that the exact exploited path is closed across the complete affected population after the canonical Harden or Restore owner supplies signed fix evidence. It does not implement or inherit the patch, configuration, authorization, isolation, or recovered-artifact result.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-E-004 verifies closure of the exact exploited path for the incident-defined population; AID-R-004 propagates the proven remediation across the wider affected fleet and future baselines.
Incident closure evidence is an input to fleet propagation, but it does not prove organization-wide rollout or recurrence prevention.

techniques.name: Compromised Durable Application Session & Agent State Teardown
techniques.description:
When compromised durable application state is identified, remove its explicitly scoped records after active runtime containment when that containment is applicable. This control remains independently applicable when no runtime execution exists.

Eviction actions
  • Delete scoped application session records without claiming bearer-token, authorization-server, or gateway-session revocation
  • Purge tainted durable conversational and agent memory
  • Remove unauthorized webhook and tool registrations
  • Cancel unauthorized queued jobs and schedule registrations

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns teardown of explicitly scoped durable application sessions, conversational or agent memory, webhook and tool registrations, nonterminal queue records, and schedule registrations after compromise. It remains applicable when no active runtime exists and never claims identity-plane revocation or active worker termination.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-E-005 deletes durable application and agent state; AID-E-001 revokes credentials, authentication sessions, principals, and delegated grants.
Application teardown does not prove identity-plane eviction, and revoked identity objects do not remove durable state that could reload or reschedule compromised behavior.

AID-E-005 removes durable queue, schedule, session, memory, and registration records; AID-E-002 terminates active processes, runs, execution leases, jobs, pods, and containers.
Deleting a durable job record does not terminate a worker that already acquired it, while runtime termination does not remove the record that can launch replacement work.

AID-E-005 removes compromised durable conversational and agent state; AID-R-003.002 restores an authority-selected clean snapshot into a new isolated namespace.
Teardown is an eviction result, while restoration must separately prove that it excludes tainted, cross-tenant, post-cutoff, secret-bearing, and credential-bearing state.

tactics.name: Restore
tactics.description: The "Restore" tactic focuses on recovering normal AI system operations and data integrity following an attack and subsequent eviction of the adversary. This phase involves safely bringing AI models and applications back online, restoring any corrupted or lost data from trusted backups, and, crucially, learning from the incident to reinforce defenses and improve future resilience.

techniques.name: Secure AI Model Restoration & Retraining
techniques.description: Restore an incident-affected model to a known-good state by either deploying an exact trusted pre-incident version or building a new remediated artifact through clean retraining when rollback is unavailable or untrustworthy.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns recovered-model readiness and release through either exact rollback or construction of a newly remediated model. It does not quarantine a suspect model, evict compromised adapters or derivatives, or remove malicious artifacts before recovery.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-R-001 restores and releases a trusted model state; AID-E-003 removes or quarantines malicious AI artifacts before recovery.
Recovery may consume AID-E-003 eviction evidence, but a successful rollback or retraining result does not prove that the compromised artifact was removed from every serving, registry, cache, or lineage path.

subTechniques.name: Versioned Model Rollback & Restoration
subTechniques.description: Restore an incident-affected model-serving release by deploying an exact known-good version from a retention-enforced immutable backup, managed-model deployment record, prompt or guardrail configuration manifest, or adapter attachment manifest authorized by an authority-signed recovery manifest, then verify the live release through an identity outside the backup-writer and deployment trust domains.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: This sub-technique owns restoration of an incident-affected model-serving release by selecting and deploying an exact authority-approved pre-incident model and serving-image pair, hosted deployment record, prompt or guardrail configuration, or adapter attachment set from immutable versioned state, then reading the live identity back through an identity outside the backup-writer and deployment trust domains before cutover. It applies only when a trustworthy prior version and trusted cutoff exist. Registry labels, endpoint names, hosted model IDs, and tool success do not authorize recovery or establish live identity. It does not quarantine a suspect model, prove adapter eviction, or build a newly remediated model.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-R-001.001 restores an exact trusted pre-incident version; AID-R-001.002 creates a newly remediated model through clean retraining or recovery learning.
Use rollback when immutable trusted prior state exists. Use AID-R-001.002 when rollback is unavailable, incomplete, or untrustworthy; AID-R-001.001 must not silently fall back to retraining.

AID-E-003.001 quarantines the suspect model; AID-R-001.001 deploys and verifies a separate known-good version.
AID-E-003.001 makes the suspect digest ineligible for serving, preserves it as incident evidence, and routes the incident to recovery. Successful rollback does not prove that the compromised model was quarantined everywhere.

AID-E-003.005 evicts compromised adapters and derivatives; AID-R-001.001 restores and verifies known-good model or adapter state.
AID-R-001.001 consumes quarantine and tombstone evidence but owns only the rollback and live-release verification. A restored deployment does not prove incident-time adapter eviction across serving, registries, caches, and lineage.

implementationGuidance: Maintain Object-Locked model versions and authority-signed digest-bound recovery manifests.
Restore an authority-selected immutable model version and read the live model and serving-image identity back through a separate deployment read path.
Restore hosted fine-tuned models, prompt/guardrail configurations, and LoRA or adapter attachments from a signed provider recovery manifest.

subTechniques.description: Restore incident-affected tools, roles, permissions, delegated authority, and action edges one policy-defined tier at a time after locally verifying every prerequisite and reading back effective runtime authority.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns policy-staged re-enablement and readback of incident-affected tools, roles, permissions, delegated authority, and action edges after recovery prerequisites pass. It does not revoke the prior authority or replace per-action runtime authorization.

techniques.name: Rapid Vector Index Rollback & Quarantine
techniques.description:
Provide fast, controlled recovery for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines after index poisoning or malicious content injection is detected. The vector index is treated as an immutable, versioned artifact.

Three-Stage Recovery
  1. Rollback — Atomically roll back to a last known-good snapshot
  2. Quarantine — Quarantine and preserve suspicious chunks for forensics while removing them from production retrieval
  3. Rebuild — Rebuild and re-promote a clean index that enforces provenance, policy, and security approvals


Goal: Restore trustworthy retrieval quality quickly while preventing re-serving tainted data.

scopeBoundary.responsibility: Owns vector namespace rollback, delete-by-ID quarantine, anti-reingestion tombstones, clean index rebuild, candidate validation, and alias cutover evidence after retrieval poisoning or malicious content injection. It does not restore authoritative source records, evict those source records, or provide ongoing production retrieval monitoring.

relatedTechniques.comparison:
AID-R-005 restores the derived vector index and serving alias; AID-R-002 restores the authoritative source records and corpora.
This control consumes restored source data and lineage findings but separately proves that tainted vectors are excluded and the rebuilt index is live.

AID-R-005 rebuilds and promotes a clean retrieval index; AID-E-003.002 identifies and evicts the exact poisoned source-record or graph population.
A vector rollback or rebuild does not prove that malicious source records can no longer be ingested again, so this control consumes the signed eviction manifest and tombstone population.

AID-R-005 performs incident-time vector-index recovery; AID-D-014 continuously monitors production RAG content, relevance, and retrieval provenance.
Detector findings can trigger recovery, but index rollback and rebuild do not replace ongoing monitoring or finding generation.
